name: Classic-Style Test 6
source: Original questions written for LSAT Trainer in the style and difficulty of recent LSATs. Not LSAC material. MIT licensed.

questions.stimulus: Glaciologist: The Vellin Glacier has retreated nearly two kilometers over the past century, and many visitors assume that the retreat began with the warming of recent decades. But survey markers left by mapmakers in the 1880s show that the glacier’s front was already pulling back then, long before that warming started. So recent warming cannot be the whole explanation for the glacier’s retreat, even if it has sped the retreat up.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the overall conclusion drawn in the glaciologist’s argument?
choices: The front of the Vellin Glacier was already pulling back in the 1880s, long before recent warming began.
Recent warming has increased the rate at which the Vellin Glacier is retreating.
Recent warming does not by itself account for the retreat of the Vellin Glacier.
The Vellin Glacier has retreated nearly two kilometers over the course of the past century.
Many visitors are mistaken in believing that the Vellin Glacier is retreating at all.
questions.explanation: The word “So” introduces the point everything else supports: recent warming cannot be the whole explanation for the retreat, which (C) restates. (B) is tempting, but the glaciologist only concedes that warming may have sped things up (“even if”); that is not asserted, let alone argued for. (A) is the evidence, and (E) distorts the visitors’ view, which is about when the retreat began, not whether it is happening.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Recent warming cannot be the whole explanation for the Vellin Glacier’s retreat.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Mapmakers’ markers show the front was already pulling back in the 1880s, before recent warming started.

breakdown.analysis: Ask which statement supports which. The conclusion is the one everything else supports. The first sentence is background: the glacier retreated and visitors blame recent warming. The 1880s markers are the evidence. “So” flags the point: warming isn’t the whole story. It’s like saying: the leak started before the new tenant moved in, so the new tenant can’t be the whole reason the ceiling is damaged. The “even if” clause is a concession, not a claim the speaker argues for.

choices.note: This is the premise. The survey markers prove it, and it in turn proves the conclusion. It sits in the middle of the support structure, not at the top.

Tempting, because it appears in the last sentence. But read the words: “even if it has sped the retreat up.” The glaciologist allows that this might be true without asserting it. A concession isn’t the conclusion.
CORRECT. “Cannot be the whole explanation” means the same thing as “does not by itself account for.” It’s what “So” introduces, and the 1880s evidence is there to support it.
Background. It sets the scene and nobody disputes it. Nothing in the argument is offered to prove it.
Distortion. The visitors think the glacier is retreating, and the glaciologist agrees. The disagreement is about when the retreat began and what caused it.

questions.stimulus: Blogger: Audiologists warn that people who are regularly exposed to loud music face an increased risk of permanent hearing loss. But my uncle has played drums in loud nightclubs several nights a week for forty years, and a hearing test last month found his hearing to be normal for his age. Clearly, audiologists have exaggerated the danger that loud music poses to hearing.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the blogger’s argument is flawed in that the argument
choices: treats one person’s experience as sufficient to show that a claim about risk across a population is exaggerated
takes for granted that what is true of musicians who play in nightclubs is true of musicians who play elsewhere
presumes, without providing justification, that the audiologists’ warnings were based on a sample that was too small
fails to specify how much exposure to loud music would be needed before hearing loss became likely
relies on the testimony of a person who has no expertise in audiology or in the study of hearing
questions.explanation: A claim about increased risk is a claim about how often hearing loss occurs across many people exposed to loud music, so one drummer with normal hearing is fully compatible with it; (A) names this. (E) is tempting, but the blogger relies on one case, not on anyone’s expert opinion, and an expert reporting the same case would make the same mistake.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Audiologists have exaggerated the danger that loud music poses to hearing.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The blogger’s uncle has drummed in loud clubs for forty years and his hearing tested normal for his age.

breakdown.analysis: So what if one drummer is fine? “Increased risk” never meant every exposed person goes deaf. It means hearing loss happens more often in the exposed group. One lucky case can’t tell you anything about how often something happens. It’s like arguing: my friend eats fast food every day and is healthy, so doctors exaggerate the risks of fast food. This is the anecdote-versus-general-claim flaw, a classic; know it. We need an answer that says one case can’t refute a claim about risk across many people.

choices.note: CORRECT. “Increased risk” is a claim about how often hearing loss shows up across many exposed people. One drummer with normal hearing fits perfectly well with that claim. A single case can’t show the risk is overstated.
The blogger never generalizes from nightclub musicians to other musicians. The jump is from one person to everyone exposed to loud music.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Jazz players in clubs rarely read sheet music, so orchestra players must rarely read it either.

choices.note: The blogger says nothing about how the audiologists reached their warning. Ironically, it’s the blogger who relies on a sample of one.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The study surely used too few people, so its findings can be dismissed.

choices.note: So? The argument doesn’t need a threshold. Even with one, a single healthy drummer still wouldn’t show the risk is exaggerated.

Tempting, because the blogger isn’t an expert. But the blogger isn’t relying on anyone’s opinion; the uncle’s hearing test is a fact. An audiologist reporting the same single case would make the same mistake.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: My neighbor, a plumber, says the new vaccine is unsafe, so it is.

questions.stimulus: Last year the health department of Corrin ran a campaign urging residents over forty to have their blood pressure checked, and it offered free checks at local pharmacies. During the following year, the number of Corrin residents being treated for high blood pressure rose by a third, even though there is no evidence that residents’ diets, weight, or exercise habits changed during that period.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain the rise in the number of Corrin residents being treated for high blood pressure?
choices: High blood pressure is considerably more common among people over forty than among younger people.
The campaign’s advertisements also urged residents to reduce the amount of salt in their diets.
Some of the residents who had their blood pressure checked as a result of the campaign learned that it was normal.
Many Corrin residents who already had high blood pressure before the campaign had not known that they had it.
In a neighboring city that ran no such campaign, the number of residents treated for high blood pressure stayed about the same.
questions.explanation: If many residents already had undiagnosed high blood pressure, the screening campaign would bring them into treatment without any change in the underlying condition, which is (D). (E) is tempting because it ties the rise to the campaign, but it only shows that the campaign made a difference; it doesn’t say how a checkup campaign could raise treatment numbers when health habits stayed the same.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Residents’ habits didn’t change, but after a screening campaign the number being treated for high blood pressure jumped by a third.

breakdown.analysis: How can more people be treated if nobody got less healthy? Easy: they were already sick and nobody knew. A campaign that gets people checked finds cases that were there all along. It’s like a new smoke detector “causing” more fire alarms: the smoke was already there, now somebody is noticing it. We need an answer that says there were hidden cases waiting to be found.

choices.note: So? This was true before and after the campaign. A constant fact can’t explain a change. It also doesn’t explain why the targeted group suddenly showed up for treatment.
This pushes the wrong way. Less salt would tend to lower blood pressure, so if anything it makes the rise more puzzling.
Interesting fact, but not relevant. People with normal readings wouldn’t be treated, so they don’t help explain more treatment.

CORRECT. If lots of residents had high blood pressure without knowing it, a campaign that gets them checked would diagnose them and put them into treatment. More treatment, same health habits. That’s the whole puzzle solved.

Tempting, because it points to the campaign as the cause. But the puzzle is how a checkup campaign could raise treatment numbers when nothing about health changed. This shows the campaign mattered; it doesn’t show how.

questions.stimulus:
Imre: Cities should be willing to name new streets after people who are still living. Honoring someone while that person can appreciate the honor makes the tribute more meaningful, and it encourages others to serve their communities.

Dana: A living person’s reputation is never settled. If someone honored with a street name is later disgraced, the city must either keep a name that embarrasses residents or go to the expense and confusion of renaming the street.
questions.stem: Imre and Dana disagree over whether
choices: honoring a person while that person is alive makes a tribute more meaningful
cities should be willing to name new streets after people who are still living
renaming a street causes expense and confusion for a city and its residents
the reputations of people who have died are more settled than those of people who are living
naming streets after people encourages residents to serve their communities more than other honors do
questions.explanation: Imre says cities should be willing to name streets after living people; Dana gives a reason against doing so, so they disagree about (B). (D) is tempting because Dana implies it, but Imre takes no position on reputations, and (E) overstates Imre’s claim while Dana never addresses it.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Imre: Name new streets after living people; the honor means more and encourages service.; Dana: A living person may later be disgraced, leaving the city with an embarrassing name or a costly renaming.

breakdown.analysis: To disagree, one speaker must say yes and the other no. Imre’s yes is explicit: cities should be willing to do this. Dana never says “no” in so many words, but the whole reply is a reason against it, and that’s how LSAT dialogues usually work. Test each choice: does Imre have a view? Does Dana? Do the views clash? Only one choice survives all three questions.

choices.note: Only Imre speaks to this. Dana never says whether a living honoree’s appreciation adds meaning; Dana worries about what happens later.

CORRECT. Imre says yes in the first sentence. Dana’s whole point is a reason not to: a living person might be disgraced, leaving the city with a bad name or a costly change. One says yes, the other says no.
Only Dana says this. Imre never mentions renaming, so we don’t know Imre’s view. To disagree, both have to take a side.
Dana hints at this, but Imre says nothing about reputations at all. One-sided, so it can’t be the point of disagreement.
Too strong for Imre. Imre says such naming encourages service, not that it does so more than other honors. And Dana doesn’t address encouragement at all.

questions.stimulus: Bookshop owner: Since the café next door closed in March, our weekday afternoon sales have dropped by a quarter, while our morning and weekend sales are unchanged. Many of our afternoon customers used to stop in to browse after leaving the café. So if a new café opens in that space, our afternoon sales will probably recover.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the bookshop owner’s argument?
choices: A new café next door would attract at least some people who would also visit the bookshop.
Most of the bookshop’s afternoon customers before March had come to the shop directly from the café next door.
A new café is likely to open in the space next door within the next year or so.
The bookshop’s afternoon sales before March were higher than they had been in any previous year.
The café that closed in March was the most popular café in the neighborhood around the bookshop.
questions.explanation: The prediction depends on a new café bringing back the browsing traffic, so the owner must assume that a new café would attract at least some people who would also visit the bookshop (A); negate it and recovery has no mechanism. (B) is tempting, but the owner says only that “many” customers came from the café, and sales could recover even if fewer than half did.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: If a new café opens next door, the bookshop’s afternoon sales will probably recover.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Afternoon sales fell by a quarter after the café closed (other sales unchanged); many afternoon customers used to browse after leaving the café.

breakdown.analysis: Why would a new café help? Only if its customers also wander into the bookshop. The old café sent browsers over, but a new one might draw a totally different crowd: commuters grabbing coffee to go, say. The owner needs at least some of the new café’s customers to stop in. Test each choice by negating it: if the negation kills the argument, it’s required.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: a new café would attract no one who would also visit the bookshop. Then a new café can’t bring sales back, and the conclusion collapses. Notice the modest wording, “at least some”; that’s typical of a right answer here.
choices.negation: A new café next door would attract no one who would also visit the bookshop.

choices.note: Tempting, because it fits the story. But the owner says “many,” not “most.” Negate it: maybe only 30 percent came from the café. A new café could still bring those people back. The argument survives, so this isn’t required.
choices.negation: It is not the case that most of the bookshop’s afternoon customers before March had come from the café.

choices.note: The conclusion is conditional: “if a new café opens.” The owner doesn’t predict that one will open. Negating this doesn’t hurt the if-then claim.
choices.negation: A new café is not likely to open in the space next door within the next year or so.

choices.note: Irrelevant. How pre-March sales compared with earlier years doesn’t bear on whether a new café would restore them. Negation does nothing.
choices.negation: The bookshop’s afternoon sales before March were not higher than in every previous year.

choices.note: Irrelevant. The old café didn’t need to be the most popular for its customers to matter to the bookshop. Negate it and nothing changes.
choices.negation: The café that closed in March was not the most popular café in the neighborhood.

questions.stimulus: For its spring exhibit, the Lindqvist Gallery used wall labels that gave only each work’s title and date, and many visitors complained that the labels were uninformative. Yet visitors to that exhibit spent more time, on average, in front of each work than visitors to any of the gallery’s previous exhibits, and a larger share of them bought the exhibit catalog.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Many of the complaints about the labels came from visitors who had also attended several of the gallery’s previous exhibits.
The catalog for the spring exhibit was priced lower than the catalogs that the gallery had produced for its previous exhibits.
Most museums provide more information on their wall labels than the Lindqvist Gallery did for the spring exhibit.
Visitors who complain about an exhibit are less likely than other visitors to return to the gallery for later exhibits.
Visitors who found the labels unhelpful looked more closely at the works and turned to the catalog for background.
questions.explanation: (E) shows how the defect produced both results: without informative labels, visitors looked longer at the works and bought the catalog to get the information the labels lacked. (B) is tempting because it explains the catalog sales, but it does nothing to explain why visitors lingered longer in front of the works.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Visitors complained that the labels were uninformative, but they spent more time per work and bought more catalogs than at any earlier exhibit.

breakdown.analysis: How could worse labels lead to more engagement? Maybe the defect helped. If the label doesn’t tell you what to think, you look harder, and if you want the backstory, you buy the book. It’s like a restaurant with a vague menu selling more of its detailed wine guide. We need an answer that explains both results: longer looking and more catalog sales.

choices.note: So? Who complained doesn’t explain why visitors stayed longer or bought more catalogs.
Tempting, because it explains the catalog sales. But it leaves the other half untouched: why would people stand longer in front of each work? Half an explanation loses to a full one.
Comparison to other museums doesn’t help. The puzzle is within this gallery: why sparse labels went with more engagement.
Irrelevant. Whether complainers come back later has nothing to do with how they behaved during this exhibit.
CORRECT. The sparse labels themselves cause both results: visitors study the works longer and buy the catalog to fill in what the labels left out. A defect that turns out to help. Paradox resolved.

questions.stimulus: Males of the leaf beetle Calopha virens have unusually long antennae, nearly twice the length of the females’. In many insect species, males locate mates by detecting airborne chemicals released by females, and longer antennae can hold more of the sensory cells that detect such chemicals. It is therefore likely that the long antennae of male C. virens serve mainly to help them find mates.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
choices: Female C. virens release airborne chemicals that males of the species can detect from several meters away.
In some other species of leaf beetle, the females have antennae that are longer than those of the males.
Male C. virens use their antennae chiefly to fence with rival males over feeding sites.
Male C. virens whose antennae have been damaged are less likely to mate than are males whose antennae are intact.
The antennae of male C. virens contain more sensory cells than do the antennae of females.
questions.explanation: The argument guesses the antennae’s function from what is true of other insects; (C) offers a different function, fencing with rivals over feeding sites, which undercuts the inference that their main use is finding mates. (D) may look like a weakener but it is consistent with the argument, and (A) and (E) actually support it.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Male C. virens’ long antennae probably serve mainly to help them find mates.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The males’ antennae are nearly twice as long as the females’; in many insect species, males find mates by sensing females’ airborne chemicals, and longer antennae hold more sensing cells.

breakdown.analysis: Just because many insects use antennae to sniff out mates, does that mean this beetle does? Maybe its antennae do something else. This is a function guess, and the classic way to weaken a function guess is to show a different job the trait actually does. We need an answer that gives the long antennae another main use.

choices.note: This helps the argument. If females give off chemicals males can detect, sensing mates with antennae looks even more likely.
Other species are a different group. What females of other beetles have doesn’t tell us what this male’s antennae are for.
CORRECT. If the males mainly use their antennae as weapons against rival males over feeding sites, then their main use isn’t finding mates. A plausible alternative function weakens the guess.
Tempting if you read it fast, but it fits the argument: damaged antennae, fewer matings. At most it’s neutral, since damage could matter for other reasons too.
So? More sensory cells is consistent with sensing mates; if anything it supports the argument. It doesn’t point to any other function.

questions.stimulus: Commentator: The Ardmore Cycling Coalition has launched a campaign urging everyone who rides a bicycle in the city to wear a helmet, on the grounds that helmets sharply reduce head injuries in collisions. Yet several of the coalition’s own officers were photographed riding without helmets during the campaign’s opening ride. Cyclists in Ardmore can therefore safely disregard the coalition’s advice.
questions.stem: The commentator’s argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it
choices: fails to consider that the photographs of the coalition’s officers may have been taken out of context
presumes that advice addressed to all cyclists in the city must be appropriate for each individual cyclist
takes for granted that cyclists who wear helmets ride no more carefully than cyclists who do not
rejects a recommendation on the grounds that those who make it do not follow it themselves
relies on the claims of an organization that has an interest in how many people take up cycling
questions.explanation: Whether coalition officers wear helmets has no bearing on whether helmets reduce head injuries; the commentator dismisses advice because its givers don’t follow it, which is (D). (A) is tempting, but even if the photos are accurate the conclusion still doesn’t follow, so the possibility that they mislead isn’t the argument’s real problem.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Ardmore cyclists can safely disregard the coalition’s helmet advice.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Several coalition officers were photographed riding without helmets at the campaign’s opening ride.

breakdown.analysis: So what if the officers ride bareheaded? That tells you about the officers, not about helmets. The reason the coalition gave, that helmets reduce head injuries, is untouched. It’s like ignoring a doctor’s advice to quit smoking because the doctor smokes; the doctor is a hypocrite, but the advice is still right. This is called tu quoque. It’s a classic; know it. We need an answer that says the argument rejects advice because the advisers don’t follow it.

choices.note: Tempting, but even if the photos are perfectly accurate, the conclusion still doesn’t follow. The real problem isn’t the evidence about the officers; it’s that their behavior is irrelevant to whether helmets work.
The commentator never reasons from the group to the individual. The argument is about the advisers, not the audience.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The campaign targets all cyclists, so it must be right for my grandmother who rides once a year.

choices.note: Nothing in the argument depends on how carefully anyone rides. Off target.
CORRECT. Whether the officers wear helmets has no bearing on whether helmets reduce head injuries. Dismissing advice because its givers don’t follow it is the tu quoque flaw, a classic; know it.
The commentator doesn’t rely on the coalition’s claims; the commentator rejects them. And no conflict of interest is mentioned.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The bike shop says cycling is healthy, so it must be.

questions.stimulus: Under the rules of the Morvan appellate court, any appeal that raises a constitutional question must be heard by the full court rather than by a three-judge panel. The appeal in the Tessaly case, which was filed last spring, has been assigned to a three-judge panel. Hence, the Tessaly appeal does not challenge the validity of a statute.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the argument follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Every appeal that does not raise a constitutional question is heard by a three-judge panel.
Every appeal that challenges the validity of a statute raises a constitutional question.
Some appeals that challenge the validity of a statute are heard by the full court.
Any appeal that is heard by the full court raises a constitutional question.
Appeals that raise a constitutional question are rarely assigned to a three-judge panel.
questions.explanation: Constitutional question → full court, so the Tessaly appeal, assigned to a panel, raises no constitutional question; adding (B), challenges a statute → constitutional question, lets the contrapositive finish the chain: no constitutional question → no challenge to a statute. (D) is the attractive reversal: it tells us what full-court appeals have, not what panel appeals lack.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Tessaly appeal does not challenge the validity of a statute.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Constitutional question → heard by the full court; the Tessaly appeal is heard by a three-judge panel, not the full court.

breakdown.analysis: The premises get us partway: Constitutional question → full court. Tessaly isn’t before the full court, so by contrapositive, Tessaly raises no constitutional question. But the conclusion is about challenging a statute, a term that appears nowhere in the premises. We need the bridge: challenges a statute → constitutional question. Then: Tessaly → no constitutional question → no challenge to a statute. The new term always has to be linked to the old one.

choices.note: This is about appeals without constitutional questions and where they go. It doesn’t mention statutes, so it can’t connect to the conclusion.

CORRECT. Challenges a statute → constitutional question → full court. Contrapositive: not full court → no constitutional question → no challenge to a statute. Tessaly is before a panel, so the conclusion follows.
“Some” is too weak to prove anything about the Tessaly appeal, and it tells us about the full court, not the panel.

Tempting, because it links the full court and constitutional questions. But it reverses the premise’s direction and still leaves statutes out. Even with it, the Tessaly appeal could challenge a statute without raising a constitutional question.
“Rarely” leaves room for exceptions, and it adds nothing the premises didn’t already say. It still never links constitutional questions to statutes.

questions.stimulus: Researchers played two groups of volunteers the same recording of a short piano piece. One group was told that the performer was a renowned concert pianist; the other was told that the performer was a first-year conservatory student. Asked to rate the performance, volunteers in the first group judged it significantly more expressive and more technically accomplished than did volunteers in the second group.
questions.stem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?
choices: Renowned concert pianists generally play more expressively than do students in their first year at a conservatory.
What listeners believe about who is performing can affect how they judge the performance itself.
Most listeners are unable to tell the difference between a skilled performance and an unskilled one.
Volunteers in the first group listened to the recording more attentively than did volunteers in the second group.
Ratings of musical performances by listeners without musical training are less reliable than ratings by trained musicians.
questions.explanation: The two groups heard the same recording and differed only in what they were told about the performer, yet rated it differently, so beliefs about the performer can affect judgments of a performance (B). (D) is tempting as a mechanism, but the study measured ratings, not attention, and (C) overstates what a labeling effect shows.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Two groups heard the same recording; 2. one was told the performer was renowned, the other that it was a first-year student; 3. the first group rated it more expressive and more accomplished.

breakdown.analysis: What’s the one thing that differed between the groups? Only the label. Same notes, same recording. So the label made the difference in the ratings. That’s all the facts support. Hard to go further: watch for answers that explain how it happened (attention, training) or that blow the result up into “people can’t hear quality at all.” We want the modest claim that belief can sway judgment.

choices.note: We don’t know this. Both groups heard the very same recording, so the study tells us nothing about how real concert pianists and students actually play.

CORRECT. The recording was identical; the only difference was what each group was told about the performer. Yet the ratings differed. So beliefs about the performer can affect judgments of the performance. Modest wording, “can affect,” is exactly what the facts support.
Too strong. Nobody was asked to compare a skilled performance with an unskilled one; everyone heard the same playing. Being swayed by a label isn’t the same as being unable to hear differences.

Tempting, because it’s a plausible mechanism. But the study measured ratings, not attention. Maybe both groups listened equally closely and the label colored their judgments. Possible isn’t supported.
New information. We aren’t told whether the volunteers had musical training, and no trained musicians were compared.

questions.stimulus: A museum should return an object in its collection to a community that claims it whenever the community can document that the object was removed without the community’s consent, even if the museum itself acquired the object lawfully and in good faith. The only exception is when returning the object would expose it to a serious risk of destruction.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?
choices: The Ferrow Museum should return a carved mask to the village of Ostel, since the villagers sincerely believe that the mask was taken from them without their consent.
The Danto Museum should not return a set of drums claimed by the Marrin community, since the drums are among the most visited exhibits in the museum.
The Lisle Museum should return a manuscript claimed by the Tavi community, since returning it to the community’s archive would pose no risk to the manuscript.
The Graye Museum should return a textile to the Senn community, which documented that it was taken without consent, even though the community has no way to protect it from rapid decay.
The Kell Museum should return a ceremonial bowl to the Avar community, which documented that the bowl was taken without consent and has a secure building ready for it.
questions.explanation: The principle requires documented removal without consent and no serious risk of destruction; (E) meets both, since the Avar community has documentation and a secure building. (D) is tempting because it has the documentation, but the textile would face rapid decay, which triggers the principle’s exception.

setup.label: Principle
setup.text: Documented removal without consent AND NOT serious risk of destruction → return the object.

setup.label: Application
setup.text: The right answer must say “return” and show 1. documentation that the object was taken without consent and 2. no serious risk of destruction if returned.

breakdown.analysis: What does a community need to get an object back? Proof, not just a belief, that it was taken without consent. And even with proof, the museum keeps the object if returning it would put it in serious danger. How the museum got it doesn’t matter. We need an answer that checks both boxes and then concludes the object should be returned.

choices.note: Sincere belief isn’t documentation. The first condition is unknown, so the principle doesn’t support returning the mask.

Popularity isn’t part of the principle. And the principle never tells a museum not to return something except in the risk case; it only says when it should. We also don’t know whether the Marrin community has documentation.
Half-right. There’s no risk, but we’re never told the Tavi community documented that the manuscript was taken without consent. Missing condition.
Tempting, because the documentation is there. But rapid decay is a serious risk of destruction, which is exactly the exception. The principle says don’t return it.
CORRECT. Documented removal without consent: check. A secure building ready to house it means no serious risk of destruction: check. So the principle says return it, and that’s the judgment.

questions.stimulus: A month-long study asked forty office workers to keep their phones outside the bedroom every night. By the end of the month, the workers reported falling asleep faster, on average, than they had during the month before the study began. The researchers concluded that keeping one’s phone out of the bedroom helps people fall asleep faster.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the researchers’ argument?
choices: Comparable workers who kept their phones in the bedroom that month fell asleep no faster than before.
Some of the workers in the study said that they found it inconvenient to keep their phones outside the bedroom at night.
Several of the workers in the study also reported waking up less often during the night than they had before.
Office workers tend to sleep fewer hours per night than do workers in most other occupations.
The month of the study was one in which the hours of daylight were growing noticeably shorter.
questions.explanation: The before-and-after comparison leaves open that something else about that month made people fall asleep faster; (A) shows comparable workers who kept their phones nearby in the same month saw no change, which rules that out. (C) is tempting but concerns a different outcome, waking during the night, and (E) suggests an alternative cause.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Keeping one’s phone out of the bedroom helps people fall asleep faster.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Workers who kept phones out of the bedroom for a month fell asleep faster than they had the month before.

breakdown.analysis: What if everyone fell asleep faster that month: cooler nights, less work stress, the novelty of being in a study? Then the phone had nothing to do with it. A before-and-after study with no comparison group can’t separate the phone from everything else that changed. We need an answer that shows people who did NOT move their phones didn’t improve.

choices.note: CORRECT. Same kind of workers, same month, phones still in the bedroom: no change. That rules out the idea that something about the month made everyone fall asleep faster, so the phone change looks like the cause.
Interesting fact, but not relevant. Whether the rule was annoying says nothing about whether it helped people fall asleep.
Tempting, because it sounds like more good news. But the conclusion is about falling asleep faster, not waking less. A different benefit doesn’t support this claim.
So? How much office workers sleep compared with other workers doesn’t touch whether moving the phone made a difference.
This hints at a different explanation, since changing daylight can affect sleep. If anything, it weakens.

questions.stimulus: Editor: Some critics hold that a translation is faithful only to the extent that it uses the word in the new language that most closely matches each word of the original. By that standard, rendering the French idiom “il pleut des cordes” word for word as “it is raining ropes” would be more faithful than rendering it “it is pouring.” That is plainly wrong, since readers of the literal version would not grasp what the original says. So the critics’ standard should be rejected.
questions.stem: The claim that a word-for-word rendering of the idiom would be more faithful plays which one of the following roles in the editor’s argument?
choices: It is the overall conclusion that the editor’s argument as a whole is designed to establish.
It is a premise that the critics themselves offer in support of their standard of faithful translation.
It is an example offered to show that some idioms cannot be faithfully translated at all.
It is a consequence of the critics’ standard that the editor uses to show the standard is mistaken.
It is a claim that the editor accepts but argues is irrelevant to evaluating the critics’ standard.
questions.explanation: The editor derives the claim from the critics’ standard (“by that standard”) and then calls it “plainly wrong,” so the claim is an absurd consequence used to sink the standard, which is (D). (B) is tempting, but the critics never offer this claim; the editor draws it out of their view in order to reject it.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The critics’ word-matching standard of faithfulness should be rejected.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: By that standard, “it is raining ropes” would count as more faithful than “it is pouring”; that result is plainly wrong, because readers wouldn’t grasp the original’s meaning.

breakdown.analysis: Does the editor believe the word-for-word version is more faithful? No: the editor calls that “plainly wrong.” The editor doesn’t believe this. It’s the absurd result the editor derives from the critics’ rule in order to sink it. It’s like answering “never tell a lie” by pointing out it would require telling a burglar where your kids are hiding.

choices.note: The conclusion is that the standard should be rejected, flagged by “So.” The editor doesn’t even believe the word-for-word claim, so it can’t be what the argument sets out to prove.

Tempting, because the claim comes from the critics’ standard. But the critics never offer it as a reason. The editor derives it from their view in order to attack it. A premise of theirs would support their standard, not embarrass it.
The editor shows the idiom can be translated perfectly well, as “it is pouring.” The point is about which translation is more faithful, not about untranslatable idioms.
CORRECT. “By that standard” marks it as following from the critics’ view, and “that is plainly wrong” marks the editor rejecting it. A consequence used to show the standard is mistaken.
The editor doesn’t accept the claim; it calls it plainly wrong. And far from being irrelevant, it’s the editor’s main weapon against the standard.

questions.stimulus: Every person registered for the Halloway Design Conference either collects a name badge at the front desk on the opening morning or has had a badge mailed in advance. A badge is mailed only to a registrant who requested mailing at least two weeks before the conference. Every registrant who collects a badge at the front desk is photographed for the conference directory. Owen Strand registered for the conference, but he was not photographed for the directory.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?
choices: Any registrant who requested mailing at least two weeks before the conference had a badge mailed in advance.
Owen Strand collected a badge at the front desk but declined to be photographed for the directory.
Some registrants who had badges mailed in advance were also photographed for the conference directory.
Owen Strand requested at least two weeks before the conference that his badge be mailed.
Owen Strand did not attend any of the conference’s sessions on its opening morning.
questions.explanation: Owen wasn’t photographed, so he didn’t collect a badge at the desk; a registrant who didn’t collect at the desk had a badge mailed; and mailing requires a request at least two weeks ahead, so (D) must be true. (A) reverses the second rule: a timely request is required for mailing, not a guarantee of it.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Registered → collects at desk OR badge mailed; 2. mailed → requested at least two weeks ahead; 3. collects at desk → photographed; 4. Owen registered and was not photographed.

breakdown.analysis: Start with Owen and chain the rules. Not photographed → (contrapositive of 3) didn’t collect at the desk. Registered and not at the desk → (rule 1) badge mailed. Mailed → (rule 2) requested at least two weeks ahead. Chain: not photographed → not desk → mailed → timely request. Watch for the answer that runs rule 2 backwards: “only to those who requested” makes the request necessary, not sufficient.

choices.note: This reverses the second rule. A timely request is required for mailing (“only to”), not a guarantee of it. Necessary isn’t sufficient.
Can’t be true. Everyone who collects at the desk is photographed, and Owen wasn’t. So he didn’t collect at the desk.
Could be true, but nothing requires it. The rules say desk collectors are photographed; they say nothing about whether anyone with a mailed badge was.
CORRECT. Not photographed → didn’t collect at the desk. Registered and didn’t collect at the desk → badge was mailed. Mailed → requested at least two weeks ahead. So Owen made a timely request.
We don’t know this. Not collecting a badge at the desk doesn’t mean he skipped the sessions; he could have arrived wearing his mailed badge.

questions.stimulus: In a recent study, volunteers studied a list of words before going to bed and were later woken during deep sleep and asked to recall the list. Brain scans taken just before waking showed intense activity in the hippocampus, a brain region involved in memory, in nearly every volunteer who recalled the list well. Thus, intense hippocampal activity during deep sleep helps people retain what they learned before sleeping.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: takes for granted that all of the volunteers studied the list of words with equal effort
overlooks the possibility that volunteers who recalled the list poorly also showed intense hippocampal activity
presumes, without providing justification, that the hippocampus is the only brain region involved in memory
fails to consider that being woken during deep sleep may make it harder to recall what one has learned
draws a conclusion about people in general from a study of volunteers who may not be representative
questions.explanation: The study reports brain activity only for good recallers; if poor recallers showed the same intense activity, that activity can’t be what distinguishes retention, so the missing comparison group is the flaw (B). (C) is tempting but the conclusion says only that hippocampal activity “helps,” which doesn’t require it to be the only region involved; (D) would lower everyone’s recall and wouldn’t explain away the link.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Intense hippocampal activity during deep sleep helps people retain what they learned before sleeping.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Nearly every volunteer who recalled the list well showed intense hippocampal activity just before waking.

breakdown.analysis: What about the volunteers who recalled the list badly? If they had the same intense activity, then the activity is just what every sleeping brain does and has nothing to do with remembering. The argument looks at only one group. It’s like noting that nearly every lottery winner bought a ticket on a Tuesday, without checking when the losers bought theirs. We need an answer that points out the missing comparison: poor recallers.

choices.note: Merely possible. Unequal effort could add noise, but it doesn’t explain why good recall goes with high hippocampal activity. And the argument never assumes equal effort.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Students who used the new textbook scored higher, so the textbook works (ignoring that some students studied much harder).

choices.note: CORRECT. The data cover only good recallers. If poor recallers’ brains showed the same activity, it can’t be what separates good retention from bad. This is the missing-comparison-group flaw.

Tempting, because it sounds like a classic overreach. But the conclusion says the activity “helps,” not that the hippocampus is the only region that matters. The argument doesn’t need that assumption.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Exercise improves mood, so people who feel down must not be exercising.

choices.note: So? If waking people up hurts recall, it hurts everyone’s recall. That doesn’t explain why good recallers had intense activity, and it doesn’t touch the conclusion.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The new test format lowered scores, so students learned less this year (ignoring that the harder format affected everyone).

choices.note: Tempting because it’s a generic study criticism. But nothing suggests these volunteers are unusual, and even a perfectly representative sample would have the real problem: no data on poor recallers.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Members of our running club love the new shoes, so most people will love them.

questions.stimulus: Judge: During the trial, juror Pell admitted that he had searched online for the defendant’s name, though he says he found nothing about the case. Even if Pell is telling the truth, he should be removed from the jury. It is essential that the public be able to see that a verdict rests only on the evidence presented in court.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the judge’s reasoning?
choices: A juror should be removed from a jury only if the juror has actually encountered information about the case outside the courtroom.
Jurors who are honest with the court about their misconduct should be treated more leniently than jurors who conceal it.
A juror should be removed if his or her conduct could lead the public to doubt that the verdict rests only on courtroom evidence.
Any juror who has lied to the court about his or her conduct during a trial should be removed from the jury immediately.
Public confidence in the courts depends more on whether verdicts are seen to be fair than on whether they are in fact accurate.
questions.explanation: The judge wants Pell removed even if his search turned up nothing, because the public must be able to see that verdicts rest only on courtroom evidence; (C) says conduct that could cast such doubt warrants removal. (D) is tempting, but the judge explicitly allows that Pell may be truthful, so a rule about lying jurors doesn’t reach this case.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Pell should be removed from the jury, even if he found nothing about the case.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Pell searched online for the defendant’s name; the public must be able to see that verdicts rest only on courtroom evidence.

breakdown.analysis: Why remove an honest juror who learned nothing? Because of how it looks. The judge cares about appearances: the public must be able to see that the verdict is clean. A principle-justify answer has to tell you to do what the conclusion says. We need a rule like: if a juror’s conduct could make the public doubt the verdict is based only on the evidence, remove the juror, even if no harm was done.

choices.note: This is the opposite. Under it, Pell stays unless he actually found something, and the judge says to remove him even if he found nothing.
Points the wrong way. If anything, it suggests Pell, who confessed, should be treated gently, not removed.

CORRECT. Searching for the defendant gives the public reason to doubt the verdict rests only on the evidence, and “could lead” means the doubt is enough even if Pell found nothing. It leads straight to removal.

Tempting, because lying jurors should go. But the judge says Pell should be removed “even if Pell is telling the truth.” A rule about liars doesn’t apply to an honest juror, so it can’t justify this conclusion.
So? A ranking of fairness against accuracy doesn’t tell the judge to do anything about Pell. It never says to remove a juror.

questions.stimulus: Café owner: Since the Tamsin Street footbridge opened in April, linking our side of the river to the office district on the far bank, our weekday lunch sales have risen by nearly a third. We changed nothing about our menu, prices, or hours during that time. So the new footbridge is what brought us the additional lunch customers.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the café owner’s argument?
choices: Several cafés far from the footbridge on the café owner’s side of the river also saw their lunch sales rise after April.
Many workers in the office district say that they would like a wider choice of places to eat lunch.
A large new residential building a block from the café filled with tenants during April.
The footbridge cost the city considerably more to build than had originally been projected by its planners.
The café’s weekend sales, when the office district is largely empty, have not risen since April.
questions.explanation: The owner credits the footbridge, which connects the café to office workers; (E) shows sales rose only when those workers are around, not on weekends, which fits the bridge explanation and cuts against a general rise in business. (B) is tempting but only shows a wish for more lunch options, not that anyone crossed the bridge, and (A) and (C) point to other causes.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The new footbridge brought the café its additional lunch customers.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Weekday lunch sales rose by nearly a third after the bridge to the office district opened; the café changed nothing else.

breakdown.analysis: Sure, sales rose after the bridge opened. But lots of things change in a few months: the season, the neighborhood, the economy. How do we tie the rise to the bridge in particular? Look for a pattern that only the bridge explains. The bridge brings office workers, and office workers are around on weekdays. We need an answer showing the gain tracks the office crowd: weekdays up, weekends not.

choices.note: This weakens. If cafés nowhere near the bridge gained too, something broader (a busier season, a better economy) may explain the rise.
Tempting, because it makes the story plausible. But wanting more choices doesn’t show these workers actually crossed the bridge to this café. Topical, but it doesn’t connect the bridge to the sales.
This weakens. New neighbors arriving the same month offer another explanation for the extra lunch customers.
Irrelevant. What the bridge cost has nothing to do with who eats lunch at the café.

CORRECT. If the bridge is bringing office workers, sales should rise only when the office district is full. Weekend sales staying flat fits that and cuts against general explanations like a busier neighborhood or a better season.

questions.stimulus: Every pottery studio in the Aldine district that sells its work to restaurants fires its pieces in a gas kiln. The Wren Street studio, which is in the Aldine district, fires its pieces in a gas kiln. So the Wren Street studio must be one of the district’s studios that sell their work to restaurants.
questions.stem: The flawed pattern of reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to that in the argument above?
choices: To be eligible for the Halden Prize, a novel must have been published within the past two years. Mira Ravel’s novel was published last year. So Mira Ravel’s novel must be eligible for the Halden Prize.

Every restaurant on Corder Street that offers outdoor seating also serves breakfast on weekends. The Blue Heron, a restaurant on Corder Street, does not serve breakfast on weekends. So the Blue Heron must not offer outdoor seating.
Every violin made in the Pazzi workshop during the last century has a maple back. This violin was not made in the Pazzi workshop during the last century. So this violin must not have a maple back.

Only members of the Harlan choir have been given keys to the rehearsal hall that the choir uses on weekday evenings. Tomas has been given a key to that rehearsal hall. So Tomas must be a member of the Harlan choir.

Most of the paintings in the Ostler collection that were acquired before 1950 are landscapes. This painting is in the Ostler collection and was acquired before 1950. So this painting must be a landscape.
questions.explanation: The argument reasons: sells to restaurants → gas kiln; Wren Street uses a gas kiln; so it sells to restaurants, treating a necessary condition as sufficient. (A) does the same once its “must” wording is translated: eligible → published recently; this novel was published recently; so it’s eligible. (D) looks like the same shape but is valid (key → member), and (C) is flawed in a different way, by negating the sufficient condition.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Wren Street studio must sell its work to restaurants.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Every Aldine studio that sells to restaurants uses a gas kiln; Wren Street uses a gas kiln.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: A → B; this one has B; so it has A (affirming the necessary condition).

breakdown.analysis: Is the kiln argument good? No. Lots of studios could use gas kilns without selling to restaurants. Sells to restaurants → gas kiln. Having the gas kiln doesn’t take you back to restaurants. It’s like saying every NBA player is tall, my cousin is tall, so he’s in the NBA. Now map each choice. Watch the wording: “must have been” and “only” both mark necessary conditions, so translate before you compare. The match has to be flawed in the same way, not just flawed.

choices.note: CORRECT. Translate “to be eligible, a novel must have been published recently”: eligible → published recently. Ravel’s novel was published recently, so it’s eligible. That treats the necessary condition as enough, exactly like the kiln argument.
Outdoor seating → weekend breakfast; no weekend breakfast; so no outdoor seating. That’s the contrapositive, and it’s valid. A valid argument can’t match a flawed one.
Tempting, because it’s flawed and uses “every.” But it’s a different flaw: it negates the sufficient condition (not Pazzi, so not maple) instead of affirming the necessary one.
Looks like the same shape, but “only members have keys” means key → member. Tomas has a key, so he’s a member. Valid.
Flawed, but differently: it treats “most” as “all.” The original’s premise is a true “every” statement; its error is running it backward.

questions.stimulus: Last year the town of Wexley began requiring shops on its main street to close by 9 p.m. Over the following twelve months, three of the street’s late-night businesses closed permanently, although none of its late-night businesses had closed in the five years before the rule took effect. Clearly, the new rule drove those three businesses out of business.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the argument depends?
choices: The three late-night businesses were the only businesses on Wexley’s main street to close permanently last year.
Most of the revenue of each of the three businesses had come from sales made after 9 p.m.
At least one of the three businesses would have stayed open had the rule not been adopted.
The town council adopted the closing rule mainly in order to reduce late-night noise on the main street.
Businesses that close by 9 p.m. generally earn less than comparable businesses that stay open later.
questions.explanation: To blame the rule for the closures, the argument must assume the closures wouldn’t have happened anyway; negate (C) and all three businesses would have closed regardless, so the rule drove none of them out. (B) is tempting, but it is stronger than needed: a business can be ruined by losing well under half its revenue.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The 9 p.m. closing rule drove the three late-night businesses out of business.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The rule took effect; within twelve months, three late-night businesses on the street closed permanently, after five years with no such closures.

breakdown.analysis: What if those three shops were going under anyway: rent hikes, a dying lease, owners retiring? Then the rule didn’t drive them out; it just happened at the same time. Any argument that blames an action for an outcome assumes the outcome wouldn’t have happened without the action. Think of a defense lawyer saying, “It would have happened anyway.” We need the answer that shuts that defense down. Test by negation.

choices.note: Too strong. Negate it: a couple of other shops also closed. The rule could still have driven out the late-night ones. The argument survives.
choices.negation: Some business on Wexley’s main street other than the three late-night businesses also closed permanently last year.

choices.note: Tempting, because it explains how the rule could hurt. But “most” is more than the argument needs. Negate it: say 35 percent of revenue came after 9 p.m. Losing that could easily sink a shop. The argument survives.
choices.negation: It is not the case that most of the revenue of each of the three businesses had come from sales made after 9 p.m.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: all three businesses would have closed last year even without the rule. Then the rule drove none of them out, and the conclusion collapses. The modest “at least one” wording is typical of a required assumption.
choices.negation: All three of the businesses would have closed last year even if the rule had not been adopted.

choices.note: Irrelevant. Why the council passed the rule has nothing to do with what the rule did to these shops.
choices.negation: The town council did not adopt the closing rule mainly in order to reduce late-night noise on the main street.

choices.note: Too general and not needed. Negate it: early-closing businesses don’t generally earn less. These particular shops could still have been ruined by losing their late hours.
choices.negation: Businesses that close by 9 p.m. do not generally earn less than comparable businesses that stay open later.

questions.stimulus: Columnist: Councilor Brandt argues that the city should stop subsidizing the municipal golf course because fewer than one resident in twenty uses it in a typical year. Yet fewer than one resident in twenty uses the city’s public boat launch in a typical year, and Brandt has repeatedly voted to expand the launch. So Brandt’s argument against the golf course subsidy cannot be accepted as it stands.
questions.stem: The columnist’s argument proceeds by
choices: attempting to show that the golf course is used by more of the city’s residents than Councilor Brandt claims
showing that a criterion Councilor Brandt relies on would, if applied consistently, count against something Brandt supports
rejecting Councilor Brandt’s position on the grounds that Brandt has a personal interest in expanding the boat launch
arguing that any two public facilities used by similar numbers of residents should receive similar levels of public funding
concluding that the golf course subsidy should be continued because the case against it has not been established
questions.explanation: Brandt’s reason is that few residents use the golf course, but the same is true of the boat launch, which Brandt supports; the columnist shows the criterion, applied consistently, would cut against Brandt’s own position (B). (C) is tempting but the columnist never alleges a personal interest, and (E) overstates the conclusion, which is only that Brandt’s argument fails as it stands.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Brandt’s argument against the golf course subsidy can’t be accepted as it stands.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Brandt’s reason is low usage (under one in twenty); the boat launch has the same low usage, yet Brandt votes to expand it.

breakdown.analysis: What’s the columnist doing? Not denying Brandt’s numbers. Taking Brandt’s own reason, low usage, and pointing at something Brandt likes that has the same low usage. If low usage is a reason to cut support, it’s a reason to cut the launch too. It’s like a parent saying “no dessert, sugar is bad” while eating cake. That’s not a proof the subsidy should stay; it’s a showing that the reason is applied inconsistently. Note the hedge “as it stands”: the conclusion is narrow.

choices.note: The columnist never disputes Brandt’s usage figure. In fact, the argument accepts it and applies the same figure to the boat launch.
choices.example: Example of this method: Brandt says few residents golf, but course records show one in eight residents played last year.

choices.note: CORRECT. Brandt’s criterion: low usage → stop public support. The boat launch meets that criterion too, yet Brandt wants to expand it. Applied consistently, the criterion would count against Brandt’s own position, so the argument can’t stand as it is.
Tempting, because it sounds like an attack on Brandt. But the columnist never says Brandt gains anything from the launch. The point is inconsistency in reasoning, not motive.
choices.example: Example of this method: Brandt owns a boat, so his votes on the launch can’t be trusted.

choices.note: Too strong. The columnist never proposes equal funding. The claim is only that Brandt’s reason doesn’t work as stated.

Overshoots the conclusion. The columnist says only that Brandt’s argument can’t be accepted “as it stands,” not that the subsidy should continue. A failed argument against something isn’t an argument for it.

questions.stimulus: Historian: It is often said that the weavers’ guild of medieval Varenna kept cloth prices high by restricting who could enter the trade. Guild records do show that the number of licensed weavers in Varenna fell by about a third between 1350 and 1400. But plague killed roughly a third of the city’s population during those same decades. So the drop in the number of licensed weavers ______.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most logically completes the historian’s argument?
choices: shows that the guild did not in fact restrict who could enter the weaving trade in medieval Varenna
was caused entirely by deaths from plague rather than by any policy of the weavers’ guild
confirms that the guild’s restrictions on entry kept cloth prices in Varenna high during that period
does not by itself provide evidence that the guild was restricting entry into the weaving trade
was smaller than the drop in the number of people practicing most other trades in Varenna
questions.explanation: The number of weavers fell by about a third, but so did the city’s population, so the share of residents who were weavers barely changed; the drop by itself is no evidence of guild restriction (D). (A) and (B) overshoot: undercutting one piece of evidence doesn’t prove the guild imposed no restrictions or that plague alone explains the drop, and (C) repeats the popular view the historian is challenging.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. People say the guild restricted entry to keep prices high; 2. licensed weavers fell by about a third, 1350–1400; 3. plague killed about a third of the population in those decades.

breakdown.analysis: Is a falling number of weavers a sign of restriction? Not if everybody’s numbers fell. A third fewer weavers in a city with a third fewer people is the same share of weavers. Watch the switch between an absolute number and a proportion; it’s a classic. The historian is pushing back on the popular view, so the blank should say the evidence doesn’t support it. But careful: “doesn’t support” is not “proves false.” We need the modest version.

choices.note: Too strong. The historian only removes one piece of evidence for restriction. The guild might still have restricted entry; the weaver count just doesn’t show it.
Too strong. The numbers match, but that doesn’t prove every lost weaver died of plague. Some could have left the trade for other reasons, including guild rules.
This repeats the popular view the historian is pushing back on. “But” signals the historian is about to undercut it, not confirm it.

CORRECT. Weavers fell by about a third; the whole population fell by about a third. So weavers per resident stayed about the same, and the drop needs no guild restriction to explain it. On its own, it’s no evidence of restriction.
New information. We know nothing about other trades, so nothing supports this comparison.

questions.stimulus: Ecologist: Barn owls, which prey heavily on voles, became considerably more numerous in the Tessel grasslands last year. Yet the vole population of the Tessel grasslands grew substantially over that same year. It follows that the voles in the Tessel grasslands had more food available to them last year than they had the year before.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the argument can be properly drawn if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: If the voles in an area have more food available in a year than the year before, their population will grow that year even if their predators become more numerous.
Most vole populations in areas where barn owls became more numerous last year declined over that year.
Whether a vole population grows depends more on the food available to it than on the number of its predators.
The vole population of the Tessel grasslands would have grown even more last year if barn owls had not become more numerous.
No vole population grows during a year in which any of its predators becomes more numerous unless its food supply also increases that year.
questions.explanation: (E) says: a predator increases AND food doesn’t increase → no growth; its contrapositive is a predator increases AND growth → more food, and the Tessel facts then yield the conclusion. (A) is the trap: it makes more food sufficient for growth, which runs the needed link backwards and leaves open that the voles grew for some other reason with no extra food.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Tessel voles had more food last year than the year before.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Barn owls, a major vole predator, increased last year; the vole population still grew substantially.

breakdown.analysis: Why must the extra growth come from food? Maybe a mild winter, less disease, fewer foxes. The argument needs a rule that rules all that out: if predators go up and voles still grow, food must have gone up. Chain: predator up AND voles grow → more food. Equivalent: predator up AND NOT more food → NOT grow. A sufficient assumption answer can be strong; it can’t be backwards. This is the SA trap where the needed link is a necessary condition and a choice offers the sufficient version.

choices.note: Tempting, because it links food, predators, and growth. But it runs the wrong way: more food → growth. We need growth → more food. With this, the voles could still have grown for some other reason without extra food.
“Most” can’t guarantee anything about the Tessel voles, which may be an exception for a reason other than food.
Vague ranking. Even if food matters more, the Tessel voles could have grown for some third reason, like a mild winter. It doesn’t force the conclusion.
Probably true, but it says nothing about food. The conclusion’s new term, food, is never linked to anything.

CORRECT. Predator increases AND no extra food → no growth. Contrapositive: predator increases AND growth → extra food. The Tessel voles had a predator increase and grew, so they had more food. The conclusion follows.

questions.stimulus: Farm association spokesperson: Some naturalists claim that the decline of the meadow skipper butterfly in the Harrow Hills is due to pesticides sprayed on nearby farms. But their only evidence is that the decline began shortly after the farms started spraying, and that sequence of events by itself hardly shows that the spraying caused the decline. So pesticides are not responsible for the meadow skipper’s decline.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes a flaw in the spokesperson’s reasoning?
choices: It treats the naturalists’ failure to establish their claim as showing that their claim is false.
It dismisses the naturalists’ claim on the grounds that the naturalists may have a bias against farmers.
It infers that one event caused another from the mere fact that the first event preceded the second.
It fails to consider that the meadow skipper’s decline may have resulted from more than one cause.
It presumes, without providing justification, that the meadow skipper population in the Harrow Hills has in fact declined.
questions.explanation: The spokesperson correctly points out that timing alone doesn’t prove the pesticides caused the decline, but then concludes that the pesticides are not responsible, treating a weak argument for a claim as proof the claim is false (A). (C) describes the naturalists’ mistake, which the spokesperson identifies rather than commits.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Pesticides are not responsible for the meadow skipper’s decline.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The naturalists’ only evidence is that the decline began after spraying began, and timing alone doesn’t show causation.

breakdown.analysis: Good point about the naturalists: timing alone doesn’t prove cause. But so what? A bad argument for a claim doesn’t make the claim false. The pesticides might still be the culprit; we just don’t know yet. The right conclusion is “unproven,” not “false.” It’s like saying: your only reason for thinking it will rain is that your knee aches, so it won’t rain. We need an answer that says the author treats a failed proof as a disproof.

choices.note: CORRECT. The spokesperson shows only that the naturalists haven’t proven their case, then concludes the opposite of their claim. Lack of proof isn’t proof of the opposite.
The spokesperson never mentions the naturalists’ motives. Wrong flaw, though the farm connection makes it feel likely.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The naturalists just dislike farmers, so their claim about pesticides can be ignored.

choices.note: Tempting, because this flaw is in the passage. But it’s the naturalists’ flaw, and the spokesperson is the one pointing it out. Watch whose reasoning the question asks about.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The decline began right after spraying started, so the spraying caused it.

choices.note: Interesting thought, but not the problem. Even if the decline had a single cause, the spokesperson would still have no grounds for ruling out pesticides.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The fire was caused by faulty wiring, so the dry weather played no part.

choices.note: The spokesperson accepts that the decline happened; that isn’t in dispute and isn’t a flaw. Everyone in the passage agrees on it.

questions.stimulus: Every beekeeper who belongs to the Alder Valley cooperative sells honey at the town’s Saturday market. Some of the cooperative’s beekeepers also make candles from the wax their own hives produce. Hence, some people who make candles from the wax of their own hives sell honey at the Saturday market.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its pattern of reasoning to the argument above?
choices: Every guide at the Corran Museum has a degree in art history. Some people with degrees in art history teach at the university. Hence, some guides at the Corran Museum teach at the university.

Most of the employees of the Fennick Bakery work early-morning shifts during the week. Some of the bakery’s employees are university students. Hence, some university students work early-morning shifts at the Fennick Bakery.

All of the moths in the Ilse collection were caught in Brazil, and all moths caught in Brazil for that collection were caught before 1950. Hence, all of the moths in the Ilse collection were caught before 1950.

Every volunteer at the Kessel Public Library has lived in Kessel County for at least a year. Some of the library’s volunteers are retired. Hence, some retired people have lived in Kessel County for at least a year.

Every licensed mountain guide in the town of Tarvik is certified in wilderness first aid. Some people certified in wilderness first aid work as lifeguards. Hence, some lifeguards are licensed mountain guides in Tarvik.
questions.explanation: The argument reasons: all A are B; some A are C; so some C are B. (D) matches exactly: all library volunteers are year-long residents, some volunteers are retired, so some retirees are year-long residents. (C) is also valid, which makes it tempting, but its all-all-all chain is a different pattern; (A) and (E) link the groups through the wrong term and are invalid, and (B) uses “most” plus “some,” which doesn’t guarantee an overlap.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Some people who make candles from their own hives’ wax sell honey at the Saturday market.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: All cooperative beekeepers sell honey at the market; some cooperative beekeepers make candles.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: All A are B; some A are C; so some C are B.

breakdown.analysis: Does it work? Yes. Take the candle-making beekeepers: they’re in the cooperative, and everyone in the cooperative sells honey, so those candle makers sell honey. The shared group (A, the cooperative) is in both premises, and the “all” premise covers it. Map each choice to letters. The match needs all A are B, some A are C, so some C are B. Being valid isn’t enough; the shape has to match.

choices.note: All A (guides) are B (art history degrees); some B teach. The “some” is about art-history graduates, not guides, so the teachers could all be non-guides. Invalid, and a different shape.
Most A work early shifts; some A are students. The students could all be in the minority who don’t work early. “Most” plus “some” doesn’t force an overlap. Invalid.
Tempting, because it’s valid too. But its shape is all A are B, all B are C, so all A are C: a chain of “alls,” not “all” plus “some.” Valid isn’t the same as parallel.
CORRECT. All A (volunteers) are B (year-long residents); some A are C (retired); so some C are B. Same terms in the same places, and valid for the same reason.
All A (guides) are B (first-aid certified); some B are lifeguards; so some lifeguards are A. The lifeguards could all be non-guides with first-aid training. Invalid.

questions.stimulus: Two years ago, Fenmark National Park closed the steepest of its three trails to the Ostra Gorge overlook and directed hikers to the other two. Since then, the number of injuries reported on the overlook trails has fallen by 40 percent, even though the number of hikers using them has not declined. So closing the steep trail has made hiking to the overlook safer.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
choices: Before the steep trail was closed, most of the injuries reported on the overlook trails occurred on that trail.
The two remaining trails are considerably longer than the steep trail was, so hikers spend more time on them.
The steep trail offered a closer view of the gorge than either of the two trails that remain open to hikers.
The park has added several new hiking trails in its forested areas, well away from the gorge, during the past two years.
Injuries on the remaining trails are far more often serious falls requiring rescue than injuries on the steep trail were.
questions.explanation: The argument measures safety by the number of injuries, but if the injuries now occurring are much more serious, hiking may not be safer overall; (E) introduces severity and weakens the conclusion. (B) is tempting because more time on a trail sounds riskier, but injuries already fell despite that, so it doesn’t undercut the result; (A) strengthens the argument.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Closing the steep trail has made hiking to the overlook safer.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Reported injuries on the overlook trails fell 40 percent after the closure, while the number of hikers didn’t decline.

breakdown.analysis: Is the number of injuries really the measure of safety? Ten twisted ankles are not worse than three falls that need a helicopter rescue. The argument counts injuries and ignores how bad they are. We need an answer that shows the remaining injuries are more serious, so fewer injuries doesn’t mean safer hiking.

choices.note: This helps the argument. If most injuries happened on the steep trail, closing it should cut injuries, just as the numbers show.

Tempting, because more time on a trail sounds like more risk. But the injury count already fell despite the longer trails. This doesn’t show the trails are less safe; if anything, it makes the drop more impressive.
Wrong dimension: the view, not safety. A worse view doesn’t make hiking more dangerous.
So? New forest trails are away from the gorge, and hiker numbers on the overlook trails haven’t dropped. This doesn’t explain the fall in overlook-trail injuries.

CORRECT. The injuries happening now are far more often serious falls needing rescue than the old ones were. Fewer injuries, but worse ones, so the trails may not be safer at all. Counts versus severity.

passages.title: Oriel Fane’s stage directions
passages.subject: humanities
passages.text:
The plays of Oriel Fane, written in the 1920s and 1930s, are notorious for their stage directions. A single direction in The Glass Orchard runs to nearly two pages, describing not only the set but the smell of the room, the history of its furniture, and what one character “has never told anyone and never will.” In an influential study, the critic Tomas Hallard argues that such passages were never meant to guide a production. Fane, he notes, published two novels before she wrote for the theater, and on his view she remained a novelist at heart who wrote for the reader in an armchair; the directions are prose fiction lodged inside a script, and directors who try to stage them misunderstand the kind of text they are handling.

Hallard’s reading has the merit of taking the directions seriously as writing, which earlier critics, who dismissed them as self-indulgent padding, did not do. But it fails to clarify what it would mean for a direction to be written “for the reader” rather than for the stage. Much of what Fane specifies is plainly theatrical: the exact moment a lamp is to dim, the number of paces between two chairs. Hallard treats the unstageable details as the essence of the directions and the stageable ones as residue, but he offers no reason for weighting them this way.

The reading also relies on an assumption Hallard never defends: that a direction can serve a production only by specifying something an audience will see or hear. Only on that assumption does the presence of unstageable material show that Fane was writing for readers. Hallard cites in support the fact that the directions in the printed editions are far longer than those in the promptbooks surviving from the premieres, productions in which Fane was closely involved. But that evidence cuts both ways.
