It is consistent with Fane’s having expanded the directions for readers, and equally consistent with her having set down in print what she had conveyed to performers by other means.

The second possibility gains support from a fact Hallard’s account cannot easily absorb. Actors who worked with Fane recalled that she read the full directions aloud at the first rehearsal of each play and never referred to them again. On this evidence, the detail about what a character has never told anyone was not meant to be shown; it was meant to be known by the actor, and to shape everything she did onstage. If so, the directions are neither instructions in the ordinary sense nor fiction for readers, but something closer to a private briefing made public, and the directors Hallard faults may have understood Fane better than he does.

passages.title: Liquidated damages and the penalty doctrine
passages.subject: law
passages.text:
When contracting parties foresee that a breach would cause losses that are hard to measure, they often agree in advance on the sum the breaching party will pay. Courts in common-law jurisdictions have long enforced such liquidated damages clauses, but only within limits. A clause that represents a reasonable estimate of the harm a breach would cause is upheld; one that sets a sum far exceeding any plausible loss, so that its evident purpose is to frighten a party into performing, is struck down as a penalty, and the injured party is left to prove its actual damages in the ordinary way.

The legal scholar Anselm Rudd has argued that this penalty doctrine is a relic. Courts enforce a contract, he notes, because its terms reflect what the parties judged to be in their interest, and a party that agrees to pay a large fixed sum for breach presumably receives something in exchange: a higher price, a faster schedule, or the contract itself, which the other side might otherwise have refused. Striking down the clause after the fact deprives the injured party of what it bargained for and hands the breaching party a benefit it never paid for. Rudd would therefore enforce any damages clause agreed to by commercial parties of comparable sophistication, however large the sum.

Rudd’s argument has real force: between well-advised firms, a court that second-guesses a negotiated figure may be substituting its own judgment of risk for theirs. Yet the argument does not clarify how a court is to know that a clause was in fact bargained over. Large firms routinely contract on standard forms that neither side reads closely, and a damages clause buried in such a form may reflect no one’s considered judgment at all. Rudd’s test of comparable sophistication describes the parties, not the transaction; it cannot distinguish a figure both sides weighed from one that one side’s lawyers inserted and the other side’s never noticed.

Rudd also takes for granted that the only parties affected by an enforced penalty are the two who signed. But a firm that must pay many times its counterparty’s actual loss may be unable to pay its other creditors, its employees, or its suppliers, none of whom agreed to anything; when a maker of hospital equipment owes a crushing sum for a two-week delay, the cost falls partly on those who depend on its continued operation. None of this rescues the doctrine’s traditional rationale, which treated penalties as objectionable simply because they coerce performance; Rudd is right that a promise backed by a strong incentive is not, for that reason, unfair. What the doctrine may protect instead is the integrity of bargaining and the interests of outsiders to the contract—purposes that suggest a narrower rule than the one courts now apply, but not its abolition.

passages.title: Probate inventories and household goods
passages.subject: social-science
passages.text:
Passage A

For most of the eighteenth century, the households of the Brennick district left almost no written trace of their daily lives. Few kept diaries, and fewer still kept accounts. Yet when a householder died leaving property to be divided, local law required two neighbors to walk through the house and list every movable object in it, with a value beside each. Some eleven thousand of these probate inventories survive for the years 1690 to 1780, and in her study of them the historian Renata Kolbe found what she calls “a quiet revolution in the kitchen.”

In inventories from the 1690s, earthenware plates appear in fewer than one household in ten; by the 1760s they appear in more than half. Mirrors, clocks, and printed books follow the same rising curve. What makes the pattern striking is that it is not confined to the prosperous. Among households whose total estate fell in the lowest third, the share owning earthenware rose almost as quickly as among the wealthiest.

Kolbe argues that this cannot be explained by rising pay, since the district’s wage records show day rates nearly flat across the period. Instead, she proposes that ordinary families changed how they worked: wives and children took in spinning and other piecework, and the added income was spent on goods that could be bought rather than made. The inventories, on this view, record not merely what people owned but a deliberate choice to labor more in order to consume more.

Whatever one makes of that interpretation, the inventories themselves offer something no other source can: a census of objects, compiled by eyewitnesses, across thousands of ordinary homes.

Passage B

Historians of ordinary people’s material lives have understandably seized on probate inventories, which appear to offer exactly what diaries and account books do not. But the impression of completeness these documents give is misleading, and conclusions about changing consumption drawn from them require more caution than they usually receive.

To begin with, inventories were not taken for everyone. The very poorest, whose possessions hardly justified the trouble of appraisal, were seldom inventoried at all. A household in the lowest third of a body of inventories is thus in the lowest third of those who owned enough to be counted—a group considerably better off than the population at large.

The people inventoried, moreover, were disproportionately old. A typical decedent had spent decades accumulating goods, so an inventory records a lifetime’s acquisitions rather than the habits of any one moment. An apparent rise in ownership across several decades may partly reflect changes in who lived long enough to leave an inventory, and at what age.

Finally, cheap items were often lumped together as “sundries,” and the threshold for listing an object separately varied among appraisers and drifted over time. An object’s first appearance in the inventories may therefore record a change in appraisers’ habits as much as a change in households’ possessions. None of this makes inventories worthless; read alongside other records, they remain indispensable. Read alone, they are an uncertain census.

passages.title: Bitter nectar in the Varrow lily
passages.subject: natural-science
passages.text:
Nectar is usually understood as a payment: a plant offers sugar so that animals will carry its pollen from flower to flower. It is therefore puzzling that the nectar of the Varrow lily, a perennial of high meadows pollinated chiefly by bumblebees, contains a bitter alkaloid that bees, when offered a choice in laboratory trials, avoid. The usual explanation has been that the alkaloid deters nectar thieves, insects that drink nectar without transferring pollen. But the botanist Leni Carrow points out that the likeliest thieves, ants, are scarce in the meadows where the lily grows, and that the few ants present seldom climb its stalks. Whatever the alkaloid does, she argues, it must do to the bees themselves.

Carrow’s proposal is that the bitterness shortens visits. A Varrow lily bears many flowers on one stalk, and a bee that finds sweet nectar tends to work its way through flower after flower on the same plant. Each such move does little for the lily: it carries pollen from one of the plant’s flowers to another, and the seeds that result are inbred and frequently fail. A bee that tastes the alkaloid, by contrast, takes a sip or two and leaves, and because it is still hungry, it flies on to another plant. Suppose a bee arrives carrying pollen from a distant lily. If it visits eight flowers, most of the pollen it leaves on the later ones will be the plant’s own, picked up from the earlier ones; if it visits only two, nearly all the pollen it leaves will be foreign.

To test the idea, Carrow’s team drained the nectar from flowers in one meadow and refilled them with a sugar solution that either contained the alkaloid at its natural concentration or lacked it. Bees on alkaloid-free plants visited an average of 6.1 flowers per plant; bees on alkaloid plants visited 2.4. When the team later used genetic markers to identify the fathers of the resulting seeds, 71 percent of the seeds from alkaloid plants proved to have been sired by other plants, against 38 percent of the seeds from alkaloid-free plants.

These results make Carrow’s account considerably more persuasive than the thief-deterrence view, at least for this species. They do not show that the benefit comes free: the team traced the parentage of seeds, not their number, and flowers that departing bees skip may go unpollinated. Moreover, the experiment was conducted in a dense stand, where a departing bee rarely had to fly more than a few meters to reach another lily. Where the plants grow sparsely, a bee repelled by bitter nectar might as readily turn to some other kind of flower altogether, carrying the lily’s pollen to no purpose. Whether the alkaloid pays for itself across the lily’s whole range thus remains an open question.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Hallard is right that Fane’s stage directions are prose fiction, but he is wrong to criticize directors who attempt to stage them.
Fane’s stage directions, long dismissed as self-indulgent padding, deserve to be read as serious prose fiction in their own right.
Hallard’s claim that Fane wrote her directions for readers rather than for productions is poorly supported and fits badly with her actual practice.
The surviving promptbooks show that Fane expanded her stage directions for readers only after her plays had first been performed.
Directors of Fane’s plays should work from the promptbooks of the first productions rather than from the much longer published texts.
questions.explanation: The author credits Hallard for taking the directions seriously but argues that his reading is undefended (second and third paragraphs) and clashes with the actors’ account of how Fane used the directions (fourth paragraph). That is C. A is the tempting half-right answer: the author does side with the directors, but denies, rather than grants, that the directions are prose fiction. B is Hallard’s view, not the author’s.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the author’s overall claim about Hallard’s reading of Fane’s stage directions.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The first paragraph sets up Hallard’s view; the turn comes at “But” in the second paragraph; the verdict is the last sentence of the fourth paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Is the passage about Fane, or about Hallard’s reading of Fane? About the reading. Paragraph 1 lays it out, paragraphs 2–3 find holes in it (no clear sense of “for the reader,” an undefended assumption, evidence that cuts both ways), and paragraph 4 adds a fact that fits badly with it. So we want: Hallard’s readers-not-stage view is weakly supported and doesn’t square with what Fane actually did. Watch for answers that adopt Hallard’s view in part.

choices.note: Tempting, because the last sentence does side with the directors Hallard faults. But the first half is the opposite of the author’s view: the author says the directions are “neither instructions in the ordinary sense nor fiction for readers.” Half right is all wrong.
This is close to Hallard’s own position, which the author credits only for “taking the directions seriously as writing.” The author never says they should be read as fiction.

CORRECT. The second and third paragraphs say the reading is undefended and its evidence cuts both ways (poorly supported); the fourth says it can’t easily absorb how Fane used the directions in rehearsal (fits badly with her practice).
The author says the promptbook evidence is consistent with this but equally consistent with another story. The passage never says the promptbooks “show” it.
The passage gives no advice to directors about which text to use. Out of scope.

questions.stem: According to the passage, earlier critics regarded Fane’s stage directions as
choices: evidence that Fane was more gifted as a novelist than as a playwright
a set of precise instructions that directors were obliged to follow closely
the most original feature of plays that were otherwise conventional in form
a record of what Fane had conveyed to her actors during rehearsals
excessive material that added little of value to the plays they accompanied
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says earlier critics “dismissed them as self-indulgent padding.” E paraphrases that. A borrows Hallard’s novelist idea and assigns it to the wrong people; D is close to the author’s own suggestion.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the passage says about how earlier critics saw the stage directions.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The first sentence of the second paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: A pure detail question. The passage says earlier critics “dismissed them as self-indulgent padding.” So we want a paraphrase of “padding”: wordy stuff that adds nothing. The traps will hand you other people’s views (Hallard’s, the author’s).

choices.note: Wrong party. The novelist idea is Hallard’s (first paragraph), and even he doesn’t rank her gifts. Earlier critics just called the directions padding.
Nobody in the passage says this. If anything, it’s close to the “ordinary sense” of instructions that the author says the directions are not.
The passage never calls the directions the plays’ most original feature, and “padding” is the opposite of praise.
Wrong party. This is close to the author’s own suggestion in the third and fourth paragraphs, not the earlier critics’ view.
CORRECT. “Self-indulgent padding” = excessive material that adds little. A straight paraphrase of the second paragraph.

questions.stem: The author’s attitude toward Hallard’s study can most accurately be described as
choices: dismissive impatience with its approach
unqualified endorsement of its conclusions
reluctant agreement with its central claim
appreciation tempered by substantial skepticism
detached neutrality regarding its merits
questions.explanation: The author credits Hallard’s reading with “the merit of taking the directions seriously as writing” but then spends most of the passage doubting it. That mix is D. A ignores the praise; C reverses the author’s verdict on the central claim.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Describe how the author feels about Hallard’s study.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The first sentence of the second paragraph (praise), then the rest of the second, third and fourth paragraphs (criticism).

breakdown.analysis: Collect the attitude words. Praise: Hallard’s reading “has the merit of taking the directions seriously.” Criticism: it “fails to clarify,” “relies on an assumption Hallard never defends,” its evidence “cuts both ways,” and the directors he faults “may have understood Fane better than he does.” So: some credit, much doubt. We need both halves.

choices.note: Too negative. “Dismissive” ignores the explicit credit the author gives Hallard in the second paragraph, and the author engages the reading carefully rather than impatiently.
Opposite. The author disputes Hallard’s conclusions.
Tempting if you read “reluctant” as the mixed part. But the author disagrees with Hallard’s central claim that the directions were written for readers. It’s the merit that’s granted, not the claim.
CORRECT. Appreciation (the reading takes the directions seriously as writing), tempered by substantial skepticism (most of the passage).
The author clearly takes sides. Neutral is wrong.

questions.stem: The primary function of the third paragraph is to
choices: identify an assumption on which Hallard’s reading depends and show that the evidence he cites fits an alternative equally well
describe the publication history of Fane’s plays in order to explain why earlier critics dismissed her stage directions as padding
concede that the textual history of Fane’s plays supports Hallard’s reading before turning to considerations that outweigh that support
present evidence that conclusively refutes Hallard’s reading and establishes that Fane wrote her directions for performers alone
propose a criterion by which critics could distinguish stage directions written for readers from those written for the stage
questions.explanation: The third paragraph names Hallard’s undefended assumption (a direction serves a production only by specifying what an audience sees or hears) and says his promptbook evidence is equally consistent with another explanation. That is A. C is the near miss: the author never concedes that the evidence supports Hallard; it “cuts both ways.” D overstates: the paragraph shows the evidence is neutral, not that it refutes him.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say what the third paragraph does in the argument.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The third paragraph, especially its first sentence and its last two sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Two moves. First sentence: Hallard’s reading “relies on an assumption Hallard never defends.” Last two sentences: his promptbook evidence “cuts both ways”; it fits a second story just as well. So: name an assumption, then neutralize his evidence. An answer that only gets one move, or makes the second move stronger than “equally consistent,” is wrong.

choices.note: CORRECT. Both moves: an undefended assumption behind Hallard’s reading, and evidence that is “equally consistent” with the alternative.
The paragraph mentions printed editions and promptbooks, but not to explain earlier critics. They appear in the second paragraph and have nothing to do with this.
Tempting, because the paragraph does discuss the textual history. But it never concedes that the evidence supports Hallard; it says the evidence “cuts both ways.”
Too strong. “Equally consistent” is not “conclusively refutes,” and the author never says the directions were for performers alone.
The second paragraph complains that Hallard never clarified this distinction, but the third paragraph doesn’t propose a criterion.

questions.stem: The author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements about the detail concerning what a character “has never told anyone and never will” (second sentence of the first paragraph)?
choices: It is an example of the stageable material that Hallard treats as a mere residue of the directions.
It can serve a purpose in performance even though nothing in a production directly represents it.
It shows that Fane intended at least some of her directions to be read only by readers of the published plays.
It was probably added to the published text of The Glass Orchard some years after the play’s premiere.
It ought to be conveyed to audiences through some means other than the dialogue spoken by the characters.
questions.explanation: In the fourth paragraph the author says this detail “was not meant to be shown; it was meant to be known by the actor, and to shape everything she did onstage.” So it serves performance without being represented, which is B. C is Hallard’s inference, which the author resists. E contradicts “not meant to be shown.”

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Predict what the author thinks about the “never told anyone” detail.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The second sentence of the first paragraph introduces the detail; the third sentence of the fourth paragraph says what the author thinks it was for.

breakdown.analysis: The detail comes back in the last paragraph. The author says it “was not meant to be shown; it was meant to be known by the actor, and to shape everything she did onstage.” So: it works in performance, through the actor, without the audience ever seeing it. We need an answer that says exactly that and no more.

choices.note: Backwards. Hallard treats the stageable details (lamp, paces) as residue. This detail is unstageable, which is what Hallard sees as the essence.
CORRECT. Known to the actor, shaping her performance, but never shown: a purpose in performance without direct representation.

Tempting, because this is the kind of detail Hallard uses for his view. But the author offers another explanation (it was for the actor), so the author wouldn’t say it shows the directions were for readers only.
The passage never dates this detail. The author argues the printed directions may record what Fane had already told performers.
Contradicts the passage: the detail “was not meant to be shown,” so the author wouldn’t want it conveyed to audiences at all.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is most analogous to the use of stage directions that the actors’ recollections (last paragraph) attribute to Fane?
choices: A composer publishes a score with detailed performance markings that the musicians are expected to consult at every rehearsal.
A novelist adapting her own novel for the stage cuts every descriptive passage that could not be shown to an audience.
At the first rehearsal, a playwright gives the actors a summary of the plot so that they can learn their lines more quickly.
A choreographer tells each dancer, once and before rehearsals, an imagined history for the role that the dance itself never depicts.
A film director writes notes on each scene for a book, published after the film’s release, intended for curious readers.
questions.explanation: The actors recall that Fane read the full directions once, at the first rehearsal, and never referred to them again; the author infers that their unstageable details were meant to be known by performers and shape their work without being shown. D matches every element. C matches the first-rehearsal timing but not the purpose: a plot summary is practical, and the plot is shown onstage.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the situation that works the same way as Fane’s use of her directions.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The second and third sentences of the fourth paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: List the features: 1. the material is told to performers; 2. once, at the start, never referred to again; 3. much of it is never shown to the audience; 4. it is meant to shape the performance from inside. The right answer needs all four. Traps match the timing or the medium but not the purpose.

choices.note: Wrong on two features: the markings are consulted at every rehearsal (Fane never referred to hers again), and performance markings directly govern what the audience hears.
This is about cutting unstageable material, the opposite of keeping it as a private briefing for performers.

Tempting: first rehearsal, given to the actors. But a plot summary to speed up memorizing lines is an ordinary practical aid, and the plot is exactly what the audience sees. Fane’s details were never shown.
CORRECT. Told to the performers once, before work begins; an imagined history the audience never sees; meant to inform how each dancer plays the role.
This is Hallard’s picture, not the actors’: notes written for readers rather than performers.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: The penalty doctrine should be abolished because it permits courts to substitute their own judgment of risk for the judgment of commercial parties.
Although Rudd’s case against the penalty doctrine has some force, it overlooks considerations that may justify keeping a narrower version of the doctrine.
The traditional rationale for the penalty doctrine remains sound, although courts have applied the doctrine to more clauses than that rationale can justify.
Because damages clauses in commercial contracts are rarely the product of genuine bargaining, courts should scrutinize every such clause closely before enforcing it.
Rudd’s argument shows that the penalty doctrine harms sophisticated commercial parties, but it fails to show that the doctrine harms anyone else at all.
questions.explanation: The author grants Rudd’s argument “real force” but raises two problems with it (how to tell a bargained clause from a buried one, and harm to outsiders) and concludes that these suggest a narrower rule, not abolition. That is B. A is Rudd’s view. C contradicts the last paragraph: the traditional rationale is not rescued.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the author’s overall conclusion about the penalty doctrine and Rudd’s attack on it.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The first sentence of the third paragraph (concession) and the last sentence of the passage (conclusion).

breakdown.analysis: Concede-and-rebut structure. Rudd: abolish the doctrine. Author: Rudd has a point, but (1) he can’t tell a bargained clause from one nobody read, and (2) he ignores outsiders. The last sentence: these purposes support “a narrower rule … but not its abolition.” So we want: Rudd has force, misses things, and a narrower doctrine survives.

choices.note: This is Rudd’s conclusion. The author concedes the point about second-guessing but rejects abolition.
CORRECT. Concession (“real force”), the overlooked considerations (bargaining and outsiders), and the conclusion (narrower rule, not abolition).
Tempting, because the author does want a narrower rule. But the last paragraph says the traditional rationale is not rescued: coercion alone isn’t unfair. The narrower rule rests on new purposes.
Too strong. The author says standard-form clauses “may reflect no one’s considered judgment,” not that damages clauses are rarely bargained, and never calls for scrutiny of every clause.
Distorts both halves. The author doesn’t say Rudd shows the doctrine harms sophisticated parties; the objection is that Rudd ignores outsiders, not that he fails to prove harm to them.

questions.stem: According to the passage, when a court strikes down a damages clause as a penalty, the injured party
choices: must prove the damages it actually suffered in the ordinary way
receives no compensation at all for the losses caused by the breach
receives whatever sum the court judges to be a reasonable estimate of the harm
may recover the stipulated sum from the breaching party’s other creditors
may still recover the stipulated sum if the breach was intentional
questions.explanation: The last sentence of the first paragraph: the injured party “is left to prove its actual damages in the ordinary way.” That is A. B overstates (it can still prove its damages); C borrows the “reasonable estimate” language from the test for upholding a clause.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what happens to the injured party when a clause is struck down.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The last sentence of the first paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Straight retrieval: struck down as a penalty → injured party “is left to prove its actual damages in the ordinary way.” Expect traps that reuse the paragraph’s other phrases.

choices.note: CORRECT. A paraphrase of “left to prove its actual damages in the ordinary way.”
Too strong. The party loses the agreed sum, not all compensation; it can still prove actual damages.
Tempting because “reasonable estimate” appears in the paragraph, but that is the test for upholding a clause. The court doesn’t substitute its own figure.
Creditors appear in the fourth paragraph as people hurt by enforcing a penalty, not as a source of payment.
Nothing in the passage turns on whether the breach was intentional.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Rudd holds that a party that agrees to pay a large fixed sum for breach
choices: is usually less sophisticated than the party that drafted the clause
expects that courts will reduce the sum if a breach in fact occurs
should be released from the clause if it later proves unable to pay
has typically failed to estimate accurately the harm its breach would cause
has presumably received something in exchange for accepting that obligation
questions.explanation: The second paragraph reports Rudd’s view that such a party “presumably receives something in exchange: a higher price, a faster schedule, or the contract itself.” That is E. A conflicts with Rudd’s focus on parties of comparable sophistication; C is closer to the author’s worry about outsiders than to anything Rudd says.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what Rudd says about a party that agrees to a large fixed sum.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The second sentence of the second paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Rudd’s premise: the party “presumably receives something in exchange.” The examples (higher price, faster schedule, the contract itself) are all things it got for agreeing. We want that, in other words.

choices.note: Rudd’s proposal is about parties of comparable sophistication. He never says the paying party is usually less sophisticated.
Nothing like this is attributed to Rudd. In fact his complaint is that courts strike such clauses down, which he thinks unfairly benefits the breaching party.
This is closer to the author’s worry in the fourth paragraph about a firm unable to pay its other creditors. Rudd says nothing of the kind.
Rudd never claims the party misjudged the harm; his point is that the figure reflects what the parties judged to be in their interest.
CORRECT. “Presumably receives something in exchange” is Rudd’s stated premise.

questions.stem: In saying that Rudd’s test of comparable sophistication “describes the parties, not the transaction” (last sentence of the third paragraph), the author most likely means that the test
choices: looks to the size of the stipulated sum rather than to the loss that the breach actually caused
applies to contracts between two firms but not to contracts between a firm and a private individual
considers who the contracting parties are but not whether the particular clause was actually negotiated
requires a court to inquire into each party’s private reasons for entering into the contract in the first place
fails to take into account whether the two contracting parties were in fact equally sophisticated
questions.explanation: The same sentence goes on to say the test “cannot distinguish a figure both sides weighed from one that one side’s lawyers inserted and the other side’s never noticed.” So it looks at who the parties are, not at whether this clause was bargained over: C. E gets it backwards, since comparable sophistication is exactly what the test does consider.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Explain what the phrase means in context.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The last sentence of the third paragraph, read with the two sentences before it.

breakdown.analysis: Read the rest of the sentence: the test “cannot distinguish a figure both sides weighed from one that one side’s lawyers inserted and the other side’s never noticed.” “Parties” = who signed (sophisticated firms). “Transaction” = what actually happened with this clause (was it negotiated?). So the test checks the signers and ignores the negotiation.

choices.note: The size of the sum is irrelevant to Rudd’s test; he’d enforce the clause “however large the sum.”
The passage never distinguishes contracts with private individuals. Invented scope.
CORRECT. Who the parties are (their sophistication) versus whether this particular clause was actually bargained over.
The opposite problem: the test asks too little about the transaction, not too much about private reasons.
Tempting because it uses the test’s own words, but backwards: comparable sophistication is exactly what the test does consider. The complaint is that it considers nothing else.

questions.stem: The author mentions a maker of hospital equipment (middle of the last paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: show that firms of comparable sophistication frequently contract on standard forms that neither side reads
provide an example of a damages clause that reasonably estimated the harm a breach would cause
suggest that penalty clauses are more common in some industries than they are in others
illustrate how enforcing a penalty can impose costs on people who never agreed to the contract
demonstrate that a delay of only a few weeks rarely causes a significant loss to the injured party
questions.explanation: The example follows the claim that a firm paying a huge penalty may be unable to pay creditors, employees or suppliers, “none of whom agreed to anything”; the cost falls on “those who depend on its continued operation.” That is D. A belongs to the third paragraph’s point, not this one.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say why the hospital-equipment example is there.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The first two sentences of the last paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: What claim does the example illustrate? The sentence right before it: Rudd assumes only the two signers are affected, but a firm paying a crushing sum may fail to pay others “none of whom agreed to anything.” The hospital example makes that concrete: patients and hospitals depend on the firm. So: costs to outsiders.

choices.note: This is the point of the third paragraph (standard forms). The hospital example is about outsiders.
The opposite: the example involves “a crushing sum” for a two-week delay, which sounds like a penalty, not a reasonable estimate.
No comparison of industries is made.
CORRECT. The example shows the cost of an enforced penalty falling on people outside the contract.
The passage doesn’t say how much the delay cost the injured party. The point is about the cost to third parties of paying the sum.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?
choices: A legal rule is described, two scholarly criticisms of it are presented, and the author argues that both of those criticisms rest on a single mistaken assumption about bargaining.
A legal rule is described, its traditional rationale is defended against a scholar’s objections, and the author concludes that courts should apply the rule to more clauses than they now do.
A scholar’s proposal for reforming a legal rule is presented, the evidence for and against the proposal is surveyed, and the author concludes that the proposal should be adopted without change.
A legal rule is described, a scholar’s case for abolishing it is set out, and the author argues that the rule’s traditional rationale, properly understood, fully answers that case.
A legal rule is described, a scholar’s case against it is set out, two gaps in that case are noted, and a basis for a narrower rule is suggested.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 describes the penalty doctrine; paragraph 2 gives Rudd’s case for abolishing it; paragraphs 3 and 4 identify two gaps (bargaining, outsiders); the last sentence suggests those purposes support a narrower rule. That is E. D is the near miss, but the author says “None of this rescues the doctrine’s traditional rationale.”

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Describe the order of moves in the passage.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: All four paragraphs; check the first sentence of each and the last sentence of the passage.

breakdown.analysis: Map it: 1. the rule (penalty doctrine); 2. Rudd says abolish it; 3. gap one: can’t tell bargained clauses from buried ones; 4. gap two: outsiders, then the traditional rationale is not rescued, but new purposes justify a narrower rule. With organization questions, one wrong element kills an answer, so check every step.

choices.note: There is only one scholar, and the author doesn’t say the criticisms share a mistaken assumption; the author partly agrees with Rudd.
Two wrong steps: the traditional rationale is not defended, and a narrower rule means applying it to fewer clauses, not more.
Wrong conclusion: the author rejects abolition, so Rudd’s proposal isn’t adopted, let alone “without change.”
Tempting: the first two steps fit. But the author explicitly says the traditional rationale is not rescued; the narrower rule rests on different purposes.
CORRECT. Rule, Rudd’s case, two gaps (paragraphs 3 and 4), and the suggestion of a narrower rule in the last sentence.

questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if accepted, would most help to justify the position the author takes in the last sentence of the passage?
choices: A court should enforce any term to which both contracting parties freely agreed, unless the term was imposed on one of them by fraud or by duress.
A court should refuse to enforce an agreed sum if, and only if, the sum was not genuinely bargained over or would seriously harm those outside the contract.
A contractual term that is designed to coerce one party into performing should never be enforced by a court, however carefully the two parties may have negotiated it.
Courts should defer to commercial parties’ own judgments about the risks of breach whenever both parties had access to competent legal advice while they negotiated the contract.
Whether a contractual term should be enforced depends chiefly on whether enforcing it would leave the breaching party able to pay all of its other debts.
questions.explanation: The last sentence says the doctrine may protect “the integrity of bargaining and the interests of outsiders,” which supports a narrower rule but not abolition. B makes exactly those two concerns the grounds, and the only grounds, for refusing enforcement: narrower than now, but not gone. A and D support Rudd’s abolition; C is the traditional rationale the author rejects; E captures outsiders only.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the principle that would back up the author’s final position: keep the penalty doctrine, but narrowed to protect bargaining and outsiders.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The last sentence of the passage, with the third paragraph (bargaining) and the fourth paragraph (outsiders).

breakdown.analysis: The position has two parts: 1. don’t abolish the doctrine (sometimes refuse enforcement); 2. narrow it to two purposes: real bargaining and protecting outsiders. So the principle should say: refuse enforcement when (and only when) the clause wasn’t really bargained or would hurt outsiders. An answer that supports abolition, or rests on coercion, or names only one purpose, fails.

choices.note: This supports Rudd: enforce whatever both sides agreed to. It would leave no room for a penalty doctrine based on bargaining quality or outsiders.
CORRECT. Both purposes from the last sentence, and only those: the doctrine survives (so not abolished) but is limited to those grounds (so narrower).
This is the traditional rationale (penalties are bad because they coerce), which the author says is not rescued.
Rudd’s position again. The author’s worry is that legal advice and sophistication describe the parties, not whether this clause was bargained over.
Tempting, because outsiders are one of the author’s concerns. But it drops the bargaining concern and makes solvency the chief test, which is narrower and different from what the author proposes.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that the author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements?
choices: Courts currently strike down too few damages clauses as penalties, especially in contracts negotiated between large and well-advised firms.
Courts should never enforce a damages clause that appears in a contract drafted on one party’s standard form.
How a damages clause came to be included in a contract can bear on whether a court should enforce it.
The penalty doctrine is justified chiefly by the fact that penalty clauses are designed to coerce parties into performing.
Rudd’s proposal would be acceptable if it were limited to contracts between firms that have no creditors other than each other.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph faults Rudd’s test because it “cannot distinguish a figure both sides weighed from one that one side’s lawyers inserted,” and the last sentence names “the integrity of bargaining” as a purpose of the doctrine. So the clause’s history matters: C. A reverses the direction (the author wants a narrower rule), and B turns “may reflect no one’s considered judgment” into “never.”

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Infer a view the author would hold.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The last two sentences of the third paragraph and the last sentence of the passage.

breakdown.analysis: Hard to prephrase, so test each answer against the author’s two concerns and the “narrower, not abolished” verdict. The author’s main complaint about Rudd is that his test ignores whether a clause was actually bargained over. So the author thinks a court can properly look at how the clause got there.

choices.note: Reversed. A “narrower rule than the one courts now apply” means striking down fewer clauses, not more. And the author grants Rudd’s point most fully for well-advised firms.
Too strong. A buried standard-form clause “may” reflect no one’s judgment; the author doesn’t say such clauses are never enforceable.

CORRECT. The author’s objection in the third paragraph is precisely that Rudd’s test ignores whether a clause was weighed by both sides; protecting “the integrity of bargaining” requires looking at that.
This is the traditional rationale, which the author says is not rescued.

Tempting, because it addresses the outsider worry. But the bargaining worry from the third paragraph would remain, and employees and suppliers are outsiders too. The author wouldn’t accept Rudd’s proposal on this limit alone.

questions.stem: Both passages are primarily concerned with
choices: explaining why the wages of ordinary workers remained nearly flat during the eighteenth century
comparing the reliability of probate inventories with that of diaries and household account books
describing the legal procedures by which the possessions of deceased householders were appraised
evaluating a particular historian’s explanation of why ordinary families chose to work longer hours
what probate inventories can reveal about changes in the possessions of ordinary households
questions.explanation: Passage A reports what one historian found in probate inventories about rising ownership of goods; passage B asks how far such inventories can support conclusions about changing consumption. The shared concern is E. D fits only passage A (passage B never mentions Kolbe or her explanation); A and C are details from passage A.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the topic both passages share.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The first paragraph of each passage.

breakdown.analysis: A “both passages” question: the answer must fit A and B. A: Kolbe’s findings from inventories (more earthenware, mirrors, clocks) and her explanation. B: inventories look complete but aren’t, so be careful drawing conclusions about changing consumption from them. Common ground: what inventories can tell us about changes in what ordinary households owned.

choices.note: Wages appear once, in passage A, as Kolbe’s reason to reject one explanation. Passage B never mentions them.
Passage B mentions diaries and account books only in passing, and neither passage compares their reliability with that of inventories.
Passage A briefly describes the appraisal procedure as background; passage B is about the inventories’ gaps, not legal procedure.
Tempting, since this is a big part of passage A. But passage B never mentions Kolbe or her explanation about work. True of one passage only.
CORRECT. A uses inventories to chart changes in possessions; B examines how reliable such conclusions are.

questions.stem: According to passage B, the threshold that appraisers used in deciding whether to list an object separately
choices: was set by local law and remained the same for every appraiser in a given district
differed from one appraiser to another and also shifted over the course of the period
was generally lower for the households of the very poorest than for wealthier households
rose steadily as cheap goods such as earthenware became more common in ordinary homes
was recorded at the head of each inventory so that later readers could take it into account
questions.explanation: The first sentence of the last paragraph of passage B says the threshold “varied among appraisers and drifted over time.” That is B. D adds a direction (“rose steadily”) and a cause the passage never gives; A borrows passage A’s mention of local law.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what passage B says about the threshold for listing an object separately.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The first sentence of the fourth paragraph of passage B.

breakdown.analysis: Retrieval: the threshold “varied among appraisers and drifted over time.” Two parts: differs by appraiser, changes over time. Watch for answers that add a direction or a cause to “drifted.”

choices.note: Contradicts passage B: the threshold varied among appraisers. The “local law” idea comes from passage A, where law required the inventory, not a threshold.
CORRECT. “Varied among appraisers” and “drifted over time,” in other words.
Passage B says the very poorest were seldom inventoried at all; it says nothing about their threshold.
Tempting because it sounds like “drifted.” But passage B never says which way it drifted or why.
Nothing in the passage says the threshold was recorded anywhere; the problem is precisely that readers can’t easily see it.

questions.stem: In passage A, the reference to the district’s wage records (first sentence of the third paragraph) serves primarily to
choices: support Kolbe’s rejection of one possible explanation of the pattern she found in the inventories
provide evidence that households in the lowest third were poorer than their inventories suggest
illustrate the kinds of written records that ordinary households in the district usually kept
show that the prices of earthenware and similar goods fell steadily during the period
suggest that the inventories understate the total income that ordinary families actually earned
questions.explanation: Kolbe says the rise in ownership “cannot be explained by rising pay, since the district’s wage records show day rates nearly flat.” The wage records rule out one explanation before she offers her own: A. C clashes with the first paragraph, which says ordinary households kept almost no records.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say why passage A mentions the wage records.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The first sentence of the third paragraph of passage A.

breakdown.analysis: Look at the “since”: the rise “cannot be explained by rising pay, since the district’s wage records show day rates nearly flat.” So the records are evidence against one explanation (higher pay), which clears the way for Kolbe’s own (families worked more).

choices.note: CORRECT. The wage records are the reason Kolbe rejects the rising-pay explanation.
That’s passage B’s worry about the lowest third, and it isn’t about wages.
Wage records are not household records, and the first paragraph says ordinary households left almost no written trace.
Prices are never mentioned. Flat wages say nothing about prices.
Kolbe does think families earned more through piecework, but the wage records are offered to show day rates were flat, not that the inventories understate income.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is a criticism that the author of passage B would be most likely to make regarding the finding about households in the lowest third that is reported in passage A?
choices: The value of the earthenware in those households was probably overstated by the appraisers who listed it.
Those households probably acquired most of their earthenware by inheritance rather than by purchase.
Those households were probably considerably more prosperous than the poorest households in the district.
The inventories of those households were probably less complete than the inventories of the wealthiest households.
Earthenware probably became common in those households only after it had become common among the wealthiest.
questions.explanation: Passage B’s second paragraph says a household in the lowest third of a body of inventories is in the lowest third “of those who owned enough to be counted—a group considerably better off than the population at large.” Applied to Kolbe’s finding, that is C. D sounds like passage B’s general skepticism but makes a rich-versus-poor completeness claim passage B never makes.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Apply passage B’s cautions to passage A’s lowest-third finding.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The last sentence of the second paragraph of passage A, and the second paragraph of passage B.

breakdown.analysis: Passage A: ownership rose almost as fast in the lowest third as among the wealthiest, so the change wasn’t confined to the prosperous. Passage B, paragraph 2, practically answers this: the lowest third of inventories isn’t the poor, because the very poorest weren’t inventoried. So B would say: those households weren’t really poor.

choices.note: Passage B worries about which items appraisers listed, not about overstated values.
Passage B never discusses inheritance. Its age point is that older people had accumulated goods over a lifetime, which isn’t the same claim.
CORRECT. Straight from passage B’s second paragraph: the lowest third of those inventoried was “considerably better off than the population at large.”

Tempting, because passage B says inventories are incomplete. But it never says poorer households’ inventories were less complete than richer ones’. Its lowest-third point is about who was counted, not how completely.
Passage A says the opposite (ownership rose almost as fast), and passage B makes no claim about timing by wealth.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately characterizes the relationship between the two passages?
choices: Passage A criticizes a historian’s use of a particular kind of record, and passage B defends that use of the record against the criticism.
Passage A describes a body of evidence and a conclusion drawn from it, and passage B argues that the same evidence supports the opposite conclusion.
Both passages draw conclusions from the same kind of record, but the conclusions in passage B concern a different region and a later period.
Passage A presents a historian’s conclusions from a kind of record, and passage B raises general concerns about that kind of record.
Passage A argues that a particular kind of record is the only reliable source on its subject, and passage B argues that it is entirely unreliable.
questions.explanation: Passage A reports Kolbe’s findings and interpretation from the Brennick inventories; passage B, without mentioning Kolbe, raises general cautions about inventories (who was counted, decedents’ age, appraisers’ habits) that bear on findings like hers. That is D. B overreaches: passage B says only that rises “may partly reflect” other factors. E is extreme on both sides: passage B calls inventories “indispensable.”

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Describe how passage B relates to passage A.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The first paragraph of each passage and the last two sentences of passage B.

breakdown.analysis: Label each passage. A: here’s what Kolbe found in inventories and how she explains it. B: inventories look complete but aren’t, so be careful. B never names Kolbe, so its concerns are general, though they hit her findings squarely. And B is cautious, not hostile: it ends by calling inventories “indispensable.”

choices.note: Reversed. Passage A doesn’t criticize Kolbe; it reports her work. Passage B is the one with reservations, and it defends nothing.
Tempting, because passage B does suggest the rise “may partly reflect” other things. But “may partly” is not “the opposite conclusion”: B never says ownership didn’t rise.
Passage B draws no conclusions about any region or period; it discusses inventories in general.
CORRECT. A: a historian’s conclusions from probate inventories. B: general concerns about probate inventories that bear on such conclusions.
Too strong, twice. Passage A says inventories offer something no other source can, which isn’t “the only reliable source,” and passage B says they are not worthless.

questions.stem: The authors of both passages would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements?
choices: Probate inventories provide information about ordinary households that is difficult to obtain from other kinds of records.
The poorest households of the period were seldom inventoried because their possessions were not worth appraising.
The rise in ownership of earthenware recorded in the inventories reflects a change in how ordinary families worked.
Probate inventories provide a complete and accurate record of all the objects found in the households they describe.
Probate inventories from the eighteenth century are more reliable than those that survive from earlier periods.
questions.explanation: Passage A ends by saying inventories offer “something no other source can”; passage B says they offer “exactly what diaries and account books do not” and remain “indispensable.” Both endorse A. B is passage B’s point alone; C is Kolbe’s interpretation, which the author of passage A sets aside (“Whatever one makes of that interpretation”) and passage B’s cautions undercut.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find a claim both authors would accept.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The last paragraph of passage A; the first and last paragraphs of passage B.

breakdown.analysis: Find common ground despite B’s skepticism. A’s author: inventories give “something no other source can.” B’s author: inventories seem to offer “exactly what diaries and account books do not” and, read with other records, “remain indispensable.” So both think inventories hold information about ordinary homes you can’t easily get elsewhere. Careful with C: it’s Kolbe’s view, and the author of A is noncommittal about it.

choices.note: CORRECT. Passage A’s last paragraph and passage B’s first and last paragraphs both credit inventories with information other records don’t give.
Only passage B says this. Passage A never discusses who wasn’t inventoried.

Tempting, because it’s the heart of passage A. But it’s Kolbe’s view, not clearly the author’s (“Whatever one makes of that interpretation”), and passage B suggests the rise may partly be an artifact.
Passage B denies this outright: the impression of completeness is “misleading.”
Neither passage compares inventories from different centuries.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true of the inventories discussed in passage A, would most reduce the force of the concern raised in the third paragraph of passage B as an objection to Kolbe’s findings?
choices: Appraisers in the 1760s were more likely than appraisers in the 1690s to list inexpensive objects individually rather than lumping them together as sundries.
Earthenware ownership rose about as fast among householders who died young as among those who died old, and the average age at death barely changed.
The number of inventories surviving from the 1760s is considerably larger than the number that survive from the 1690s, when record keeping was less systematic.
Many of the householders in the lowest third of the inventories owned no land, and most of them earned their living chiefly through wage labor.
Most of the householders whose estates were inventoried had lived in the district for their entire adult lives and died there in old age.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph of passage B says inventoried people were disproportionately old, so a rise in ownership over decades may partly reflect changes in who lived long enough to be inventoried, and at what age. B removes both routes: the rise appears at every age, and the age mix didn’t shift. A bears on passage B’s fourth paragraph (appraisers’ habits) and would actually support that different concern.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the fact that would neutralize passage B’s age concern as applied to Kolbe’s data.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The third paragraph of passage B; the second paragraph of passage A for Kolbe’s findings.

breakdown.analysis: Pin down the concern first. Passage B, paragraph 3: inventories record lifetime accumulation by mostly old people, so a rise across decades “may partly reflect changes in who lived long enough to leave an inventory, and at what age.” To defuse it, show the rise isn’t an age effect: e.g., it happened among the young too, and the age at death didn’t change. Traps will address passage B’s other concerns (appraisers, who was counted) or just confirm that decedents were old.

choices.note: Wrong concern. This is about appraisers’ habits (passage B’s fourth paragraph), and it would make that concern stronger, since later appraisers would list cheap items that earlier ones lumped together.
CORRECT. If ownership rose equally among those who died young and old, and the age at death barely moved, the rise can’t be explained by a shift in the age of those inventoried.
More inventories later doesn’t touch the age concern. It might affect sampling, but not who was old.
This is about the lowest third and about wealth, passage B’s second-paragraph concern, and it doesn’t defuse even that.
Tempting because it talks about age. But it confirms the decedents were old rather than showing the age mix stayed constant, so the concern stands.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: The alkaloid in the Varrow lily’s nectar is best explained as a defense against insects that drink nectar without carrying pollen.
Carrow’s experiment shows that the bitter nectar of the Varrow lily increases cross-pollination wherever the species happens to grow.
Because bumblebees avoid bitter nectar, lilies that produce it receive fewer pollinator visits and therefore set fewer seeds than other lilies.
Carrow’s view that the lily’s bitter nectar promotes cross-pollination by shortening bee visits is well supported, though its scope is uncertain.
Nectar is better understood not as a payment to pollinators but as a means by which plants control the movements of their visitors.
questions.explanation: The passage poses a puzzle, sets aside the thief-deterrence answer, explains and tests Carrow’s visit-shortening account, and ends by calling it persuasive for this species while leaving open whether it pays off everywhere. That is D. B is the main trap: the last paragraph refuses to say “wherever the species grows.” A is the view the passage sets aside.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the main point, including the author’s final verdict.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The first and last paragraphs for the frame; the second and third paragraphs for Carrow’s account and test.

breakdown.analysis: What does the author actually conclude? Not just “Carrow is right.” The last paragraph says her account is “considerably more persuasive” than the rival, “at least for this species,” then raises two doubts: the cost in seed number, and sparse stands. So: Carrow’s explanation is well supported, with a reservation about its reach. Main-point answers must match the author’s level of confidence.

choices.note: This is the “usual explanation” the first paragraph sets aside because ants are scarce where the lily grows.
Tempting, because the experiment supports Carrow. But “wherever the species happens to grow” is exactly what the author won’t say: sparse stands are an open question.
The passage never says alkaloid plants set fewer seeds; it raises that as an untested possibility. And it isn’t the main point.
CORRECT. Carrow’s mechanism (shorter visits → more outcrossing), its support (the third paragraph), and the reservation about scope (the last paragraph).
Too broad. The passage is about one lily, not a new theory of nectar; the “payment” idea is background that sets up the puzzle.

questions.stem: According to the passage, in Carrow’s experiment, bees on plants whose flowers had been refilled with the alkaloid-free solution
choices: visited fewer flowers per plant than did bees on the plants whose flowers held the alkaloid
typically took only a sip or two of nectar from each flower before leaving the plant
visited more than twice as many flowers per plant as did the bees on the alkaloid plants
left mostly foreign pollen on the flowers they visited after the first two on each plant
often left the stand altogether to forage on other kinds of flowers growing nearby
questions.explanation: The third paragraph gives 6.1 flowers per plant for alkaloid-free plants against 2.4 for alkaloid plants, more than twice as many: C. A reverses the numbers; B describes bees on alkaloid plants.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the experiment showed about bees on the alkaloid-free plants.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The second sentence of the third paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Numbers: alkaloid-free 6.1 flowers per plant; alkaloid 2.4. 6.1 ÷ 2.4 ≈ 2.5, so “more than twice as many” works. Expect reversals and descriptions of the other group.

choices.note: Reversed. Bees on alkaloid-free plants visited more flowers (6.1 vs. 2.4).
Wrong group. “A sip or two” is how the second paragraph describes bees that taste the alkaloid.
CORRECT. 6.1 is more than twice 2.4.
Backwards. The second paragraph says a bee visiting many flowers leaves mostly the plant’s own pollen on the later ones.
The experiment reports nothing about bees leaving the stand; the last paragraph raises that only as a possibility in sparse stands, and for repelled bees.

questions.stem: In using the phrase “to no purpose” (second-to-last sentence of the passage), the author most probably means that the lily’s pollen in such a case
choices: would be carried to lilies growing too far from the source plant to be fertilized by it
would be left on the plant’s own flowers, where it would yield only inbred seeds
would be eaten by the bee rather than being carried to any other flower at all
would reach another lily only after its capacity to fertilize had begun to decline
would end up on flowers of other species, which it cannot fertilize, and so produce no seeds
questions.explanation: The sentence says that in sparse stands a repelled bee “might as readily turn to some other kind of flower altogether, carrying the lily’s pollen to no purpose.” The pollen goes to flowers of a different kind, where it fertilizes nothing: E. B describes the problem the alkaloid is supposed to prevent, not this one.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Explain what “to no purpose” means in its sentence.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The second-to-last sentence of the passage (the fourth sentence of the last paragraph).

breakdown.analysis: Read the whole sentence: where lilies are sparse, a bee repelled by bitter nectar “might as readily turn to some other kind of flower altogether, carrying the lily’s pollen to no purpose.” Where does the pollen go? To a different kind of flower. Why is that pointless? Lily pollen can’t fertilize another species. Traps will describe other ways pollen can be wasted.

choices.note: The passage never says distance itself prevents fertilization; the problem is the bee goes to a different kind of flower.
Tempting, because inbreeding is the waste discussed in the second paragraph. But this sentence is about a bee leaving for another kind of flower, the opposite of staying on the same plant.
The passage never says bees eat pollen.
Pollen aging is never mentioned. Invented mechanism.
CORRECT. The bee turns to “some other kind of flower altogether,” so the lily’s pollen lands where it can’t fertilize anything.

questions.stem: The passage provides information that most helps to answer which one of the following questions?
choices: Why does Carrow doubt that the alkaloid serves mainly to protect the lily’s nectar from ants?
At what concentration does the alkaloid begin to deter bumblebees from drinking the lily’s nectar?
Do Varrow lilies growing in sparse stands produce less of the alkaloid than lilies in dense stands do?
How many seeds did the alkaloid plants in Carrow’s experiment produce compared with the alkaloid-free plants?
Which insects other than ants have been proposed as the nectar thieves that the alkaloid might deter?
questions.explanation: The first paragraph answers A: ants are scarce in the lily’s meadows, and the few present seldom climb its stalks. D is the strongest trap; the last paragraph says the team traced “the parentage of seeds, not their number,” so the passage specifically lacks this answer.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the question that the passage actually answers.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The fourth sentence of the first paragraph; also check the third and last paragraphs for the traps.

breakdown.analysis: Go answer by answer and ask: can I point to a sentence that answers this? Watch for questions on the passage’s topic that the passage leaves open, especially ones the passage flags as open.

choices.note: CORRECT. The first paragraph gives Carrow’s reasons: the likeliest thieves, ants, are scarce in these meadows, and the few present seldom climb the stalks.
The experiment used the alkaloid only “at its natural concentration.” No threshold is given.
Sparse stands come up only as an open question about bee behavior; the passage gives no alkaloid levels by stand density.

Tempting, because the experiment and seeds are discussed in detail. But the last paragraph says the team traced the parentage of seeds, “not their number.” The passage specifically doesn’t answer this.
The passage names ants as the likeliest thieves and mentions no others.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most strengthen the proposal described in the second paragraph?
choices: Bumblebees that taste the alkaloid at one Varrow lily tend to avoid all Varrow lilies for the rest of that foraging trip.
Varrow lilies whose nectar naturally contains little alkaloid have a larger share of seeds that fail to mature than do typical lilies.
The alkaloid is also present in the leaves of the Varrow lily, where it discourages grazing by deer and other mammals.
In laboratory trials, bumblebees offered only alkaloid-laced nectar for several days come to drink it as readily as sweet nectar.
In the stand that Carrow studied, the Varrow lily flowered at the same time as several other plants pollinated by bumblebees.
questions.explanation: Carrow’s chain: alkaloid → shorter visits → less pollen moved within a plant → fewer inbred seeds, which “frequently fail.” If low-alkaloid lilies have more failed seeds, the chain’s predicted payoff shows up in nature: B. A weakens the account, since a bee that shuns all Varrow lilies won’t carry pollen to another one.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the fact that best supports Carrow’s visit-shortening account.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The second paragraph, with the experiment in the third paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Lay out the chain: bitter → bee leaves after a sip or two → flies to another plant → more foreign pollen, fewer inbred seeds → fewer seeds that fail. A strengthener can confirm any link, or confirm the predicted outcome in natural plants. Watch for answers that cut the chain (bees leave the species entirely) or give the alkaloid some other job.

choices.note: This weakens the account: if a repelled bee avoids every Varrow lily, it won’t carry pollen to another one, so bitterness wouldn’t increase cross-pollination.
CORRECT. Less alkaloid → longer visits → more inbred seeds → more seeds that fail. Finding that pattern in natural plants supports the proposal’s payoff.
An extra job for the alkaloid elsewhere in the plant tells us nothing about what it does in nectar.
If anything this weakens: bees that get used to the taste would stop cutting visits short.
Tempting as context, but it doesn’t bear on the mechanism. If anything, nearby alternatives raise the sparse-stand worry from the last paragraph.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the passage?
choices: The alkaloid is likely to be present at higher concentrations in Varrow lilies that grow in sparse stands than in those that grow in dense stands.
Bumblebees are unable to detect the alkaloid in Varrow lily nectar until they have already drunk a substantial amount of the nectar containing it.
In Carrow’s experiment, the alkaloid plants produced more seeds in total than did the alkaloid-free plants growing in the same meadow.
Had bees lingered on the alkaloid plants as long as on the others, a smaller share of those plants’ seeds would probably have been outcrossed.
Most of the seeds produced by the alkaloid plants in Carrow’s experiment were sired by pollen from the plants that bore them.
questions.explanation: On Carrow’s account, which the author finds persuasive, outcrossing rises because bees visit fewer flowers per plant. If bees had stayed as long on alkaloid plants as on alkaloid-free ones, that cause would be removed and the outcrossed share should fall: D. C is the main trap: the passage says the team counted parentage, not seed numbers. E reverses the figures: 71 percent were sired by other plants.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the claim best supported by the passage.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The second paragraph (the mechanism) and the third paragraph (the results).

breakdown.analysis: Hard to prephrase, so test each choice. The passage’s causal story: fewer flowers visited per plant → more foreign pollen → higher outcrossed share (71% vs. 38%). Ask what follows if you remove the cause. D does exactly that, in different words (“lingered … as long” = visited as many flowers). Watch for answers that reverse a percentage or assert something the passage says wasn’t measured.

choices.note: No data on alkaloid levels by stand density. The passage suggests the alkaloid may pay off less in sparse stands, which, if anything, points the other way.
Contradicts the passage: a bee that tastes the alkaloid takes “a sip or two and leaves,” so it notices quickly.

Tempting, because more outcrossing sounds like more seeds. But the last paragraph says the team traced “the parentage of seeds, not their number,” and even suggests skipped flowers may go unpollinated.
CORRECT. Carrow’s mechanism makes the shorter visit the cause of the higher outcrossed share; remove the shorter visit and the share should drop toward the alkaloid-free plants’ level.
Reversed. 71 percent of the alkaloid plants’ seeds were sired by other plants, so most were not self-sired.

questions.stimulus: Folklorist: For generations, Tiller coast boatbuilders built their fishing boats only from oak planks. Some observers claim that younger builders, who use plywood and epoxy, have broken with that tradition. But these builders keep the hull shapes their predecessors developed, and most learned those shapes from older builders. A craft tradition lives in its designs and its handed-down knowledge as much as in its materials. So the younger builders are continuing the tradition, not breaking with it.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the overall conclusion drawn in the folklorist's argument?
choices: For generations, Tiller coast boatbuilders built their fishing boats only from oak planks.
A craft tradition consists more in its designs and handed-down knowledge than in the materials its practitioners use.
Most of the younger Tiller coast builders learned the traditional hull shapes directly from older builders.
The younger Tiller coast builders who work in plywood and epoxy are continuing the coast's boatbuilding tradition.
The observers who say the younger builders have broken with tradition are focusing on materials rather than on designs.
questions.explanation: The folklorist rejects the observers' claim and concludes, in the last sentence, that the younger builders are continuing the tradition (D); the first sentence is background and the hull shapes, the training, and the general claim about traditions are support. B is the tempting distortion: the folklorist says a tradition lives in designs and knowledge 'as much as' in materials, not 'more,' and that general claim is a premise anyway.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The younger builders are continuing the Tiller coast boatbuilding tradition, not breaking with it.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: They keep the traditional hull shapes; most learned those shapes from older builders; a craft tradition lives in its designs and knowledge as much as in its materials.

breakdown.analysis: What is the folklorist trying to prove? Ask which statement supports which. The conclusion is the one everything else supports. The first sentence (oak planks for generations) is background; ignore it. The second sentence is the view the folklorist opposes. The hull shapes, the training, and the general claim about traditions all point at one thing: the young builders haven't broken with the tradition. That's the last sentence, flagged by 'So.' We need an answer that says the plywood-and-epoxy builders are carrying the tradition on.

choices.note: Background. It explains why anyone would think plywood is a break, but nothing in the argument is offered to prove it, and it isn't the point.
Tempting, because it's the general principle the argument leans on. But it's a premise, not the conclusion, and it's distorted: the folklorist says 'as much as,' not 'more than.'
A premise. It's one of the two pieces of evidence that the younger builders keep the tradition alive.
CORRECT. This is the 'So' sentence. The hull shapes, the training, and the principle about traditions are all offered in support of it.
The folklorist never diagnoses why the observers think what they do. This invents a claim about the opponents; it may be implied, but it isn't what the argument sets out to prove.

questions.stimulus: Parent: Child psychologists claim that toddlers who are read to every day go on to develop larger vocabularies than toddlers who are not. But my neighbor read to her son every night from the time he was born, and at age three he still spoke fewer words than most children his age. Clearly, the psychologists have overstated the benefits of reading to toddlers.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the parent's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: presumes, without providing justification, that reading aloud is the only way to build a toddler's vocabulary
treats a single case that does not fit a general tendency as grounds for rejecting a claim about that tendency
relies on the report of a neighbor who has no expertise in child development or in measuring vocabulary
fails to consider that toddlers who are read to every day may also be spoken to more often by their parents
takes for granted that a child's vocabulary at age three predicts the size of that child's vocabulary later in life
questions.explanation: The psychologists' claim is about a general tendency, and one child who doesn't fit it does nothing to show the tendency is overstated, so B describes the flaw. C is tempting, but the neighbor is reporting simple facts about her own son (how often she read, how many words he says), which need no expertise; the problem is drawing a general conclusion from one case.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The psychologists have overstated the benefits of reading to toddlers.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Psychologists say daily reading tends to produce larger vocabularies; the neighbor's son was read to nightly and still has a small vocabulary at three.

breakdown.analysis: So what if one kid didn't fit? A tendency is a claim about averages, and averages survive exceptions. It's like arguing: my uncle smoked every day and lived to 90, so doctors exaggerate the risks of smoking. That's the anecdote-versus-general-claim flaw, and it's a classic; know it. We need an answer that says the parent uses one case to knock down a claim about a general pattern.

choices.note: The parent never says reading is the only way to build vocabulary. If anything, the parent is doubting that reading matters much. Describes an assumption the argument doesn't make.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Liam's vocabulary is small, so his parents must never have read to him.

choices.note: CORRECT. The psychologists describe what tends to happen. One boy who bucks the trend is exactly what you'd expect even if the tendency is real and strong.

Tempting, because 'not an expert' sounds like a credibility problem. But the neighbor is only reporting how often she read and how many words her son says. You don't need a degree for that. The problem is the leap from one case, not the source.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: My barber says this new heart drug is dangerous, so it must be.

choices.note: This is a real causal worry, but it would cut against the psychologists, not against the parent. It isn't a flaw in the parent's reasoning.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Kids who are read to have big vocabularies, so reading causes big vocabularies.

choices.note: The parent's point doesn't depend on predicting later vocabulary. The parent uses the three-year-old's vocabulary as a current snapshot. Irrelevant to the gap.

questions.stimulus:
Hollis: The Brayford community garden should assign its plots by lottery each year rather than letting gardeners renew their plots indefinitely. Under the current system, residents who have been on the waiting list for years may never get a plot.

Teresa: But renewal rewards gardeners who spend years enriching their plots' soil. A yearly lottery would hand that soil to newcomers and give no one a reason to improve a plot. The garden should keep its current system.
questions.stem: Hollis and Teresa disagree over whether
choices: some residents have been waiting for years for a plot in the Brayford community garden without receiving one
gardeners who have spent years enriching the soil of their plots deserve some reward for that effort
the Brayford community garden should stop letting gardeners renew their plots and assign plots by yearly lottery
a lottery is a fairer way to distribute scarce goods than a waiting list is
gardeners who receive plots through a lottery would have less reason to improve the soil than current gardeners have
questions.explanation: Hollis says the garden should replace renewal with a yearly lottery; Teresa says it should keep the current renewal system, so they disagree over C. A and E are each addressed by only one speaker (Hollis on the waiting list, Teresa on incentives), and B is something only Teresa speaks to.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Hollis: switch to a yearly lottery, because people on the waiting list may never get a plot; Teresa: keep renewal, because it rewards soil improvement and a lottery would kill the incentive to improve plots.
