breakdown.analysis: To disagree, one speaker must say yes and the other no. Find the one question both of them answer. Hollis: should the garden switch to a lottery? Yes. Teresa: 'The garden should keep its current system.' No. Everything else (the waiting list, the soil, the incentives) is a reason only one of them gives. We need an answer about whether to replace renewal with a lottery.

choices.note: Only Hollis speaks to this. Teresa never denies that people have waited for years; she just thinks the soil argument wins. She could agree with A and still oppose the lottery.
Only Teresa takes a position. Hollis never says soil-improvers don't deserve reward; he could grant it and still prefer a lottery for fairness to the waiting list.
CORRECT. Hollis: yes, switch to a lottery. Teresa: no, keep renewal. Both commit, in opposite directions.
Neither compares a lottery with a waiting list. Hollis compares a lottery with indefinite renewal. This swaps in a different comparison.
Tempting, because it's Teresa's main reason. But Hollis says nothing about incentives to improve the soil, so we can't say he rejects it.

questions.stimulus: In the Marro Valley, farmers who stopped plowing their fields and instead planted directly into the previous year's crop residue found that, within a few years, their soil held considerably more water after a rain and lost less of it during dry spells. Yet in years with cool, wet springs, these farmers' fields produced smaller harvests than nearby plowed fields did.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: The residue left on unplowed fields keeps the soil cold in spring, and seeds sprout poorly in cold, soggy soil.
Plowed fields in the Marro Valley lose considerably more topsoil to wind and water erosion than unplowed fields do.
Most Marro Valley farmers who stopped plowing did so mainly to cut the fuel and labor costs of preparing their fields.
In years with hot, dry summers, unplowed fields in the Marro Valley produce larger harvests than plowed fields do.
Soil that holds more water after a rain generally supports a larger population of earthworms, which help aerate it.
questions.explanation: Holding more water sounds like a pure benefit, yet the unplowed fields do worse in cool, wet springs. A explains this: the residue keeps the soil cold, and cold, soggy soil is bad for sprouting seeds, so the extra moisture becomes a liability in exactly those springs. D is tempting because it is about yields, but it describes dry years and leaves the wet-spring puzzle untouched.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: No-till fields hold more water after rain, but in cool, wet springs they yield less than plowed fields.

breakdown.analysis: Why would better water retention hurt? Notice the specific condition: cool, wet springs. In those years more water isn't what the crop needs. We need an answer showing something about no-till fields that hurts the crop specifically when springs are cold and wet. That lets both facts be true at once.

choices.note: CORRECT. The residue keeps the soil cold, and wet, cold soil stops seeds from sprouting. In a cool, wet spring the no-till field is both colder and wetter, so it does worse. Both facts now fit.
Another advantage of not plowing. It makes the lower wet-spring harvests more puzzling, not less.
Explains why farmers switched, not why their harvests drop in wet springs. Motive is irrelevant to the yields.
Tempting, because it's about harvests. But it talks about hot, dry summers. The puzzle is about cool, wet springs, and this says nothing about them.
Another benefit of water-holding soil. It deepens the puzzle instead of resolving it.

questions.stimulus: At the start of this season, the Brask Mountain ski area began stationing an instructor at the top of each beginner run to steer novice skiers toward slopes suited to their ability. So far this season, the ski patrol has treated a third fewer injured beginners than it had by this point last season. Clearly, stationing the instructors has reduced injuries among beginning skiers.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the argument?
choices: Most of the injuries that beginning skiers suffer at Brask Mountain occur on runs designated for beginners.
Not all of the drop in beginner injuries would have occurred had the instructors not been stationed.
The instructors stationed at the beginner runs are more experienced than most of the other instructors at Brask Mountain.
No other ski area in the region reduced injuries among beginners this season without taking similar steps.
Injuries to beginning skiers are the most frequent and most costly kind of injury that the ski patrol treats.
questions.explanation: To credit the instructors with the drop, the argument must assume the drop would not have happened anyway; B states exactly that in modest form, and if it were false (the whole drop would have occurred regardless) the instructors reduced nothing. A is tempting, but if most beginner injuries happened elsewhere, steering skiers at the top of beginner runs could still prevent some injuries.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Stationing instructors at the beginner runs reduced injuries among beginners.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Instructors were stationed this season; beginner injuries treated are down a third from the same point last season.

breakdown.analysis: So injuries fell after the change. Would they have fallen anyway? Maybe the snow was better, or fewer beginners came this year. The argument needs the drop to be at least partly due to the instructors. This is a counterfactual-cause assumption: the outcome wouldn't have happened without the action. We need an answer that says the drop isn't entirely something that would have happened anyway.

choices.note: Not required. If most beginner injuries happened on other runs, instructors steering people at the top of beginner runs could still prevent some. Negating it doesn't break the argument.
choices.negation: At least half of the injuries beginners suffer occur somewhere other than the beginner runs.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: the entire drop would have happened even without the instructors. Then the instructors reduced nothing, and the conclusion collapses. Classic defender answer.
choices.negation: All of the drop in beginner injuries would have occurred even if no instructors had been stationed.

choices.note: Not required. Ordinary instructors could steer novices just fine. Negating it does nothing to the causal claim.
choices.negation: The stationed instructors are no more experienced than most other instructors at the area.

choices.note: Too strong, and about other ski areas. Another area could have cut injuries some other way without telling us anything about Brask. Negating it is harmless.
choices.negation: At least one other ski area in the region reduced beginner injuries this season without taking similar steps.

choices.note: The argument is only about whether beginner injuries fell because of the instructors. How they rank against other injuries is irrelevant.
choices.negation: Injuries to beginners are not both the most frequent and the most costly kind the patrol treats.

questions.stimulus: Researchers who spent two years observing capuchin monkeys in the Kessa Forest found that groups whose members spend more of each day grooming one another have fewer violent conflicts within the group than other groups do. A monkey being groomed typically lies still, often with its eyes half closed. Grooming, the researchers conclude, must ease tension among group members and thereby help prevent conflict.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the researchers' argument?
choices: Capuchin groups in several other forests also spend a large share of each day grooming one another.
Grooming also allows capuchins to remove ticks and other parasites from parts of one another's bodies they cannot reach.
Some violent conflicts within capuchin groups occur between monkeys that had groomed each other earlier that same day.
The Kessa Forest groups that groom the most are, on average, neither larger nor smaller than the groups that groom least.
Capuchins seldom groom monkeys they have recently fought with, so frequent fighting leaves fewer pairs willing to groom.
questions.explanation: The researchers infer that grooming prevents conflict from a correlation between the two. E suggests the causation runs the other way: fighting suppresses grooming. C is tempting but only shows that grooming doesn't prevent every conflict, which is consistent with its reducing conflict overall; D, by ruling out group size, actually helps the argument.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Grooming eases tension and so helps prevent conflict.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Groups that groom more have fewer violent conflicts.

breakdown.analysis: More grooming goes with less fighting. But which causes which? Maybe groups that fight a lot just don't groom, because monkeys don't groom their enemies. That's reversed causation, and it's the first thing to check whenever a correlation becomes a cause. We need an answer that shows conflict could be driving the grooming numbers.

choices.note: Other forests grooming a lot tells us nothing about whether grooming reduces conflict. Irrelevant.
Grooming can have more than one function. Removing parasites doesn't stop it from also easing tension. Doesn't hurt the argument.
Tempting. But the claim is that grooming helps prevent conflict, not that it prevents every fight. A few exceptions are fine for a 'tends to' effect.
This rules out group size as a hidden factor. That helps the argument, if anything.
CORRECT. If fighting reduces grooming, then the correlation is explained in reverse: groups that fight a lot groom less because few pairs are on good terms. Grooming need not prevent anything.

questions.stimulus: According to a policy of the Arbor Street Preschool, a child should be moved into the next age group's classroom ahead of schedule if the child's parents request the move and, in addition, either the child's current teacher recommends the move or the child scores well above the typical level on the school's readiness assessment.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the policy stated above?
choices: Maya's teacher recommends moving her ahead, and Maya scored well above the typical level on the readiness assessment. So Maya should be moved ahead.
Theo's parents requested that he be moved ahead, but his teacher does not recommend the move. So Theo should not be moved ahead.
Priya's parents asked that she be moved ahead, and she scored well above the typical level on the readiness assessment. So Priya should be moved ahead.
Lena scored well above the typical level on the readiness assessment, and her teacher has told her parents that she is ready. So Lena should be moved ahead.
Sam's parents requested that he be moved ahead, and Sam scored at about the typical level on the readiness assessment. So Sam should be moved ahead.
questions.explanation: The policy requires a parental request plus at least one of two further conditions (teacher recommendation or a well-above-typical score); Priya has the request and the score, so moving her ahead conforms (C). A and D satisfy the 'or' conditions but lack the required parental request, and B wrongly draws a 'should not' conclusion from a policy that only says when a child should be moved.

setup.label: Principle
setup.text: Parents request AND (teacher recommends OR score well above typical) → move the child ahead.

setup.label: Application
setup.text: Find the child who meets the request condition plus at least one of the two others, and who is judged 'should be moved ahead.'

breakdown.analysis: The right answer has to satisfy every condition: 1. a parental request; 2. either a teacher recommendation or a well-above-typical score; 3. a verdict of 'should be moved.' Watch for answers that check the 'or' box but skip the request, and for 'should not' verdicts. The rule only tells you when to move a child; it never tells you when not to.

choices.note: Tempting, because it satisfies both of the 'or' conditions. But there's no parental request, and the request is required.

The policy says when a child should be moved. It never says a child who fails the conditions should not be. Treating the rule as 'only if' is the reversed-conditional trap. (And Theo might still score well above typical; we aren't told.)
CORRECT. Request: yes. Score well above typical: yes, which satisfies the 'or.' Verdict: should be moved. Every condition is met. The teacher's view doesn't matter once the score condition is met.
Great score and a supportive teacher, but nobody says the parents requested the move. The required condition is unknown.
Request: yes. But 'about the typical level' isn't 'well above,' and there's no teacher recommendation. The 'or' condition fails.

questions.stimulus: At Tarrant Freight, a shipment may be sent by express air only if the customer has prepaid the express surcharge for it. Any shipment containing lithium batteries must travel by sea unless it has been inspected by a certified handler. No shipment travels both by express air and by sea. Last week, a shipment for the customer Holloway contained lithium batteries and was sent by express air.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?
choices: Holloway's shipment was inspected by a certified handler, and Holloway prepaid the express surcharge for it.
Holloway's shipment did not travel by sea, and it was not inspected by a certified handler before it was sent.
Every shipment at Tarrant Freight that has been inspected by a certified handler is sent by express air.
Holloway has prepaid the express surcharge on every shipment it has ever sent through Tarrant Freight.
Every shipment at Tarrant Freight for which the express surcharge was prepaid was sent by express air.
questions.explanation: Express air requires a prepaid surcharge, so Holloway prepaid it; and since the shipment went by air it did not go by sea, so the lithium-battery shipment must have been inspected (otherwise it would have had to go by sea). A combines both results. B contradicts the second result, E reverses the first rule, and D stretches a fact about one shipment to all of Holloway's shipments.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Express air → surcharge prepaid; 2. Lithium AND not inspected → sea; 3. Not both air and sea; 4. Holloway's shipment: lithium, sent by express air.

breakdown.analysis: Run the shipment through the rules. Express air → surcharge prepaid (rule 1). Express air → not sea (rule 3). Contrapositive of rule 2: not sea → not lithium OR inspected. It had lithium, so it was inspected. Chain: air → not sea → inspected; air → prepaid. We need an answer that says it was inspected and the surcharge was prepaid.

choices.note: CORRECT. Prepaid follows directly from rule 1. Inspected follows because a lithium shipment that wasn't inspected would have had to go by sea, and this one went by air instead.
The first half is true, but the second half is the opposite of what follows. Uninspected lithium must go by sea, and this one didn't.
Inspection only removes the sea requirement. It doesn't send anything by air. This invents a rule.
We know about one shipment. Nothing tells us about Holloway's other shipments. Too broad.
This reverses rule 1. Prepaying is required for express air, not a guarantee of it. Reversing a conditional is the most common trap; watch for it.

questions.stimulus: Ethicist: The Alvaro Foundation recently sold a painting from its collection to raise money for its art-education programs. The painting was donated decades ago by a collector who expressed no wishes about whether it could ever be sold, and the money from the sale will fund programs that serve the foundation's stated mission. Some members of the public object to the sale, but the foundation acted properly.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the ethicist's reasoning?
choices: An institution should never sell a donated work while members of the public continue to object to the sale.
An institution acts properly whenever most members of the public support the decisions it makes about its collection.
If the proceeds from selling a donated work are used for purposes outside an institution's mission, the sale is improper.
Selling a donated work is proper if the donor did not restrict its sale and the proceeds advance the institution's mission.
A donor who expresses no wishes about a gift's future gives up any claim to control how the institution uses the gift.
questions.explanation: The ethicist concludes the sale was proper because the donor set no restriction and the proceeds serve the mission; D says exactly those two conditions make a sale proper. C is tempting because it mentions the mission, but it only says when a sale is improper, so it can never establish that this sale was proper; E covers the donor condition but never says the sale was proper.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The foundation acted properly in selling the painting.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The donor expressed no wishes about selling it; the proceeds fund programs serving the foundation's mission; some of the public objects.

breakdown.analysis: A principle-justify answer has to tell you to do what the conclusion says. The conclusion is 'the sale was proper.' The facts offered are: 1. no donor restriction; 2. proceeds serve the mission. So we want: no restriction AND proceeds serve the mission → sale is proper. The public objection is the view being brushed aside, so the right principle shouldn't depend on it.

choices.note: Opposite. Public objections exist here, so this principle would condemn the sale.
We're told some people object, but not whether most support the decision. And the ethicist's reasons are the donor's silence and the mission, not public opinion. Wrong basis.
Tempting, because it mentions the mission. But it only tells you when a sale is improper. It can't establish that a sale is proper. Watch the direction: a rule for 'improper' can't justify 'proper.'
CORRECT. Its two conditions are exactly the two facts the ethicist gives, and its verdict, 'proper,' is exactly the conclusion.
Covers the donor's silence but says nothing about the mission or about whether the sale was proper. Partial match; it never reaches the conclusion.

questions.stimulus: Editor: Some anthology editors propose that a poem be included in a school anthology only if it was widely read in its own time. But many poems now regarded as central to the literary canon found few readers when they were first published. If the proposal were adopted, then, school anthologies would have to omit many of the very poems that students most need to know. Editors should therefore reject the proposal.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the role played in the editor's argument by the claim that school anthologies would have to omit many of the very poems that students most need to know?
choices: It is the main conclusion of the editor's argument, which the other statements are offered to support.
It is offered as support for the claim that many canonical poems found few readers when first published.
It is a claim that the editor attributes to the anthology editors who favor adopting the proposal.
It is a general principle that the editor uses to evaluate proposals about what school anthologies include.
It is an undesirable consequence that the editor claims would follow from adopting the proposal.
questions.explanation: The editor derives this result from the proposal (via the fact that many canonical poems were little read at first) and uses it as the reason to reject the proposal, so it is an undesirable consequence of adopting the proposal (E). A is tempting because the claim is itself supported, but it in turn supports the final sentence, the recommendation to reject the proposal, which is the main conclusion.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Editors should reject the proposal.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Many canonical poems had few readers at first; so the proposal would force anthologies to omit poems students most need to know.

breakdown.analysis: Where does the claim come from, and where does it go? It follows from the proposal plus the fact about canonical poems ('then'), and it supports 'Editors should therefore reject the proposal.' So it's a bad result that the editor says the proposal would produce, used as the reason to reject it. The editor doesn't want this outcome; it's the absurd result used to sink the rule.

choices.note: Tempting, because the claim has support of its own. But it then supports the last sentence. The main conclusion is 'reject the proposal,' and this is the reason for it.
Backward. The fact about canonical poems supports this claim, not the other way around.
The proposal's supporters would never say this; it's the editor's objection to them.
It's a specific predicted result, not a general principle for evaluating proposals.
CORRECT. It's a consequence the editor says would follow from adopting the proposal, and the editor treats it as unacceptable, which is why the proposal should be rejected.

questions.stimulus: In the Corran electricity market, wholesale prices during evening hours have fallen sharply since several large battery storage facilities began operating two years ago. These facilities charge their batteries at midday, when abundant solar generation makes electricity cheap, and sell the stored power in the evening. So the battery facilities are responsible for the drop in evening prices.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?
choices: Battery storage facilities have also been built over the past two years in several other electricity markets in the region.
In the past two years, evening demand in Corran has not fallen, and no other new evening supply has begun operating.
Several of the battery storage facilities in the Corran market are owned by companies that also operate large solar farms.
Evening wholesale prices in the Corran market were higher three years ago than at any point in the preceding five years.
Consumers in the Corran market use considerably more electricity during the evening hours than they use around midday.
questions.explanation: The argument attributes the fall in evening prices to the batteries, so it is strengthened by ruling out other explanations; B eliminates the two most obvious ones, falling demand and new supply. E is tempting because it explains why evening power is valuable, but it gives no reason to think the batteries rather than something else caused the price drop.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The battery facilities caused the drop in evening prices.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Evening prices fell after the batteries began operating; the batteries buy cheap midday power and sell it in the evening.

breakdown.analysis: Prices fell after the batteries arrived. But what else could lower evening prices? Less evening demand, or some other new evening supply (say, a new gas plant or imports). Strengtheners often work indirectly by ruling out the alternative cause. We need an answer that says those other usual suspects didn't happen.

choices.note: Other markets building batteries tells us nothing about what caused Corran's price drop. We'd need to know what happened to prices there, and we don't.
CORRECT. Prices fall when demand falls or supply rises. This rules out lower demand and any other new supply, leaving the batteries as the best explanation.
Who owns the batteries doesn't affect whether they lowered prices. Irrelevant.
About prices before the batteries arrived. A high starting point might even suggest prices were due to fall back on their own. Doesn't help.
Tempting, because it shows evening power matters. But the argument already assumes there's an evening market; this does nothing to show the batteries caused the drop.

questions.stimulus: Soil scientist: When farmers apply more nitrogen fertilizer than their crops can absorb, the excess acidifies the soil, harms beneficial soil microbes, and washes into nearby streams as nitrate, where it feeds algae blooms. Farmers who care about the long-term health of their soil, therefore, should not apply nitrogen fertilizer to their fields at all.
questions.stem: The soil scientist's argument is flawed because it
choices: fails to consider that some farmers may not care much about the long-term health of their soil
takes for granted that because excessive amounts of nitrogen fertilizer are harmful, any amount of it is harmful
draws a conclusion about the health of soil from evidence that concerns only the health of nearby streams
confuses a condition that is necessary for maintaining healthy soil with one that is sufficient for doing so
takes for granted that harm to soil microbes is more serious than the harm caused by algae blooms
questions.explanation: The evidence concerns only fertilizer beyond what crops can absorb, yet the conclusion rules out applying any nitrogen fertilizer; B names that leap from excess to any amount. C is tempting because streams are mentioned, but the scientist also cites soil acidification and harm to microbes, so the evidence is not only about streams.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Farmers who care about their soil's long-term health should apply no nitrogen fertilizer at all.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Nitrogen fertilizer beyond what crops can absorb acidifies the soil, harms microbes, and pollutes streams.

breakdown.analysis: Every harm listed comes from the excess, the amount crops can't absorb. So what about the amount they can absorb? It's like arguing: too much water drowns a houseplant, so never water it. This is the 'excess is harmful, so never use any' overgeneralization. We need an answer that says the argument moves from too much to any.

choices.note: The conclusion is only about farmers who do care. Farmers who don't are outside the argument. Irrelevant.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Everyone who wants clean teeth should floss, so every person in town will start flossing.

choices.note: CORRECT. The evidence is about excess fertilizer; the conclusion bans all of it. Harmful in large amounts doesn't mean harmful in any amount.
Tempting, because streams are mentioned. But the scientist also cites acidified soil and harmed microbes, which are about soil. The premise objection is false.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Factory runoff kills fish in the river, so the factory is ruining the farmland.

choices.note: Sounds technical, but there's no necessary-versus-sufficient confusion here. The argument never says what is needed for healthy soil.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Watering is necessary for a healthy lawn, so if I water mine it will be healthy.

choices.note: The argument never ranks harms. It doesn't need microbes to matter more than algae; any one of the harms would do.

questions.stimulus: In a study, researchers asked the parents of 400 kindergartners how often their children engaged in unstructured, imaginative play at home. The children whose parents reported the most imaginative play scored highest, on average, on a test of self-control given at school. The researchers concluded that imaginative play helps young children develop self-control.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the researchers' reasoning?
choices: Some of the children whose parents reported little imaginative play also scored very well on the test of self-control.
The test of self-control used in the study has also been given to kindergartners in several other countries.
Imaginative play has also been found in other studies to help young children develop larger vocabularies and social skills.
The parents in the study were not told in advance that their children would later be given a test of self-control.
Children who already have good self-control are better at sustaining long games of make-believe and so play them more.
questions.explanation: The researchers infer that play builds self-control from a correlation between them. E gives the reverse explanation: self-control makes children better at, and so more drawn to, sustained imaginative play. A is tempting, but a few exceptions are fully compatible with an average effect.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Imaginative play helps young children develop self-control.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Children whose parents reported the most imaginative play scored highest, on average, on a self-control test.

breakdown.analysis: Play and self-control go together. Fine. But which way does the arrow point? Maybe kids who can already control themselves are the ones who can keep a long game of pretend going. When a correlation is turned into a cause, look for reversed causation. We need an answer that says self-control could be producing the play.

choices.note: Tempting, because it sounds like a counterexample. But the finding is about averages, and some exceptions are expected. Doesn't touch the causal claim.
Where else the test is used is irrelevant to whether play caused the scores.
Another possible benefit of play. It neither helps nor hurts the claim about self-control.
This removes a possible source of bias in the parents' reports. If anything it helps the study.
CORRECT. Reversed causation: if self-control lets kids sustain imaginative games, the correlation is explained without play building self-control.

questions.stimulus: Many people believe that the hospitals with the longest emergency-room waits are the worst managed. But wait times depend heavily on how many patients arrive, and hospitals with strong reputations tend to attract patients from well beyond their own neighborhoods. Moreover, a well-run emergency room treats the most urgent cases first, which lengthens the waits of patients with minor complaints. So a long average wait at a hospital's emergency room ______.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most logically completes the argument?
choices: is a reliable sign that the emergency room is poorly managed, whatever the hospital's reputation may be
results mainly from the emergency room's failure to treat the most urgent cases before minor ones
is not, by itself, good evidence that the emergency room is poorly managed
shows that the hospital has a stronger reputation than any other hospital in its region
could be shortened considerably if emergency rooms stopped giving priority to the most urgent cases
questions.explanation: The author pushes back on the popular view by giving two ways a long wait can coexist with, or even reflect, good management (a strong reputation drawing patients, and treating urgent cases first). The fitting conclusion is the modest C. A repeats the popular view the author is rejecting, and D overstates what a long wait shows.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Popular view: longest waits = worst managed; 2. Waits depend on how many patients come, and strong-reputation hospitals draw extra patients; 3. Good ERs treat urgent cases first, which lengthens minor-complaint waits.

breakdown.analysis: The 'But' tells you the author is pushing back on the popular view. Both reasons show a long wait can happen at a well-run ER. That doesn't prove long-wait ERs are well run; it only shows the wait alone doesn't prove bad management. We need a modest blank-filler: a long wait isn't, on its own, good evidence of poor management. Watch for the trap that repeats the popular view.

choices.note: This is the popular view the author is arguing against. Classic trap for complete-the-argument questions.
Opposite. The author says good ERs do treat urgent cases first, and that this lengthens waits.
CORRECT. Both reasons show a long wait can come from popularity or good triage, so a wait alone doesn't show poor management. Modest, and exactly what the premises support.
Too strong. A strong reputation is one possible cause of long waits; it doesn't follow that a long wait proves the strongest reputation in the region.
The author treats urgent-first triage as a feature of good management, not something to drop. And nothing supports 'considerably.'

questions.stimulus: Regulator: The Dunmore Power Company has asked permission to raise its residential electricity rates, citing recent increases in fuel prices. But Dunmore buys all of its electricity from other companies under long-term contracts that fix the price it pays, so its costs of supplying electricity have not risen significantly. Its request should therefore be denied.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the regulator's argument can be properly drawn if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: A utility's request to raise its rates should be granted if the utility's costs of supplying electricity have risen significantly.
Long-term contracts at fixed prices are the most economical way for a utility to obtain the electricity it sells.
Increases in fuel prices raise the costs of the companies that sell electricity to utilities under long-term contracts.
A utility's request to raise its rates should be granted only if the utility's costs of supplying electricity have risen significantly.
Most utilities that request permission to raise their rates cite recent increases in fuel prices as their main reason.
questions.explanation: The regulator establishes that Dunmore's costs have not risen significantly and concludes the request should be denied, so the needed link makes rising costs a necessary condition for granting: grant → costs rose; costs didn't rise → deny. D supplies exactly that. A is the attractive trap: it makes rising costs sufficient for granting, which says nothing about what to do when costs have not risen.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Dunmore's request to raise its rates should be denied.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Dunmore buys power at fixed contract prices, so its costs of supplying electricity have not risen significantly.

breakdown.analysis: Premise: costs did NOT rise significantly. Conclusion: request should NOT be granted. We need a bridge: costs not risen → don't grant. Its contrapositive: grant → costs rose. In words: grant only if costs rose. Chain: no significant cost rise → (bridge) → deny. Watch for the sufficient-condition version, which looks almost identical.

choices.note: Tempting, because it differs from the right answer by one word. 'Grant if costs rose' tells you what to do when costs rose. Ours didn't, so this rule is silent. Using it to deny would be negating a conditional.
Whether fixed contracts are economical has nothing to do with whether the request should be denied. Irrelevant.
If anything this hints Dunmore's suppliers might raise prices later. It doesn't connect 'costs didn't rise' to 'deny.'
CORRECT. Grant → costs rose significantly. Dunmore's costs didn't rise, so by the contrapositive the request should not be granted. The conclusion follows.
What most utilities cite tells us nothing about whether this one's request should be denied.

questions.stimulus: Six months ago, Garrow Housewares began packing its fragile goods in molded-pulp inserts instead of the foam it had used for years. In the six months since the switch, customers have filed 25 percent fewer damage claims for fragile goods than in the six months before. So the pulp inserts protect fragile goods better than the foam did.
questions.stem: The answer to which one of the following questions would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Did the number of fragile goods the company shipped change substantially between the two six-month periods?
Are molded-pulp inserts less expensive to buy and easier to dispose of than the foam inserts they replaced?
Do customers say they prefer receiving goods packed in molded pulp rather than in foam?
Have other housewares companies also switched from foam to molded-pulp inserts in the past year?
Are damage claims for fragile goods more common at Garrow than damage claims for other kinds of goods?
questions.explanation: Fewer claims means better protection only if the company shipped a comparable number of fragile goods in both periods; if shipments fell by a third, a 25 percent drop in claims would mean a higher damage rate. A asks exactly that. B raises a different dimension (cost and disposal), and E compares fragile goods with other goods rather than the two periods.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Pulp inserts protect fragile goods better than foam did.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Damage claims for fragile goods fell 25 percent in the six months after the switch.

breakdown.analysis: Is the number of claims really the measure of protection? Only if the number of shipments stayed about the same. Fewer claims could just mean fewer fragile items shipped. That's the count-versus-rate gap. We need a two-sided question: if shipments held steady, the argument gets stronger; if shipments dropped a lot, it falls apart.

choices.note: CORRECT. If shipments stayed level, fewer claims means a lower damage rate (helps). If shipments fell sharply, the drop in claims could be all volume (hurts). Either answer matters.
Wrong dimension. Cost and disposal are about whether the switch was worthwhile, not whether pulp protects better.
Customer taste in packaging says nothing about how well it protects. Irrelevant.
Other companies switching doesn't tell us whether pulp works better at Garrow.
Compares the wrong things. The argument compares fragile-goods claims across two periods, not fragile goods with other goods.

questions.stimulus: Over the past decade, the number of people holding deer-hunting licenses in Merrin State has fallen by about a third, and state wildlife officials expected the annual deer harvest to fall along with it, since fewer hunters would presumably kill fewer deer. Instead, the number of deer killed by licensed hunters in the state each year has risen steadily.
questions.stem: Each of the following, if true, helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above EXCEPT:
choices: The fee for a deer-hunting license in Merrin State has more than doubled over the past decade.
The state's deer population has grown substantially over the decade, making deer far easier for hunters to find.
Over the decade the state lengthened its deer-hunting season and raised the number of deer each hunter may take.
Most of the people who stopped hunting in Merrin State were people who rarely killed a deer in any season.
Hunters who remain active in Merrin State now use scopes and trail cameras that make them far more successful.
questions.explanation: The puzzle is fewer hunters but more deer killed; B, C, D, and E each give a reason the remaining hunters could kill more deer or the departing ones were not contributing many kills. A only explains why fewer people hold licenses, which is the half of the puzzle that needs no explanation, so it does nothing to resolve it. D is the tempting one to pick, but it does help: it shows the hunters who left weren't the ones killing deer.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: The number of licensed deer hunters fell by a third, but the number of deer killed each year rose.

breakdown.analysis: In an EXCEPT question, four answers resolve the paradox and the right answer doesn't. How can fewer hunters kill more deer? More deer to find, more days or bigger limits, better gear, or the people who quit weren't killing deer anyway. Prephrase the odd one out: something that explains only one side of the puzzle, or is irrelevant. The commonest trap here is an answer that explains just the drop in hunters.

choices.note: CORRECT. Higher fees explain why fewer people hunt. But the drop in hunters isn't the puzzle; it's the starting fact. This says nothing about why more deer are being killed, so it doesn't resolve anything.
Resolves it. More deer that are easier to find means each remaining hunter can kill more.
Resolves it. A longer season and bigger limits let each remaining hunter take more deer.

Tempting to pick, because it doesn't explain a rise by itself. But it does help: if the people who quit weren't killing deer, the drop in hunters shouldn't lower the harvest, which removes the expectation the paradox rests on.
Resolves it. Better equipment makes the remaining hunters more successful, so fewer of them can kill more deer.

questions.stimulus: Primatologist: Researchers have watched the gibbons of the Selan Reserve for more than two thousand hours and have never seen one use a tool, and some have concluded that Selan gibbons do not use tools. But this conclusion is unwarranted, since nearly all of those hours of observation took place in the high canopy during daylight. Thus, Selan gibbons probably do use tools, but only in places and at times when they have not been observed.
questions.stem: The primatologist's reasoning is flawed in that it
choices: draws a general conclusion about all Selan gibbons from observations made only in the canopy during daylight
fails to consider that gibbons in other reserves might use tools in the very places where they have been observed
treats the weakness of the evidence for a conclusion as grounds for thinking that the conclusion is probably false
presumes, without providing justification, that researchers would recognize tool use by a gibbon if they happened to see it
relies on the reports of other researchers whose expertise in observing and interpreting gibbon behavior has not been established
questions.explanation: The primatologist correctly shows that the other researchers' evidence doesn't establish that the gibbons never use tools, but then concludes the gibbons probably do use tools, which nothing supports; C describes this. A is the attractive trap: it describes the flaw in the other researchers' reasoning, which the primatologist points out, not the primatologist's own mistake.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Selan gibbons probably do use tools, just where and when no one has watched.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The 'no tools' conclusion rests on observation almost entirely in the daytime canopy, so it is unwarranted.

breakdown.analysis: The first move is fine: watching only the daytime canopy can't show gibbons never use tools. But then the primatologist jumps to 'they probably do.' Showing an argument fails doesn't prove its conclusion false. It's like saying: your evidence that my car is fine is weak, so my car is probably broken. Rebutting an argument isn't the same as proving the opposite. We need an answer that says weak evidence for 'no tools' is treated as support for 'tools.'

choices.note: Tempting, because this is a real flaw in the story. But it's the other researchers' flaw, and the primatologist is the one pointing it out. Read the stem: we want the primatologist's mistake.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: We only surveyed people at the gym, and none of them smoke, so nobody in town smokes.

choices.note: Gibbons in other reserves are irrelevant to what the Selan gibbons do.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Our gibbons never use tools, so no gibbons anywhere do.

choices.note: CORRECT. The primatologist shows the 'no tools' evidence is inadequate, then treats that inadequacy as reason to think the gibbons probably do use tools. Lack of proof isn't proof of the opposite.
The argument doesn't need this. Even if researchers would always recognize tool use, the leap from 'unproven' to 'probably true' would still be the problem.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The inspectors saw no cracks, so the bridge has none; they would surely spot any crack.

choices.note: The primatologist doesn't rely on the researchers' expertise; the point is where they looked, not how well they watched. Attacks-the-source answers are usually traps.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The researchers never studied primatology formally, so their findings about gibbons can be ignored.

questions.stimulus: Every macaque troop on Pemba Ridge that forages in the farmers' orchards has learned to raid storage sheds. No troop that has learned to raid storage sheds is left unmonitored by the wildlife service. So any troop on Pemba Ridge that the wildlife service leaves unmonitored does not forage in the farmers' orchards.
questions.stem: The pattern of reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to that in the argument above?
choices: Every song on the Larkin album that was recorded before 1990 features a string section. No song that features a string section was chosen for the radio edit. So any song on the album that was chosen for the radio edit was recorded before 1990.

Every student in Ms. Ortega's class who completed the reading passed the quiz. Some students who passed the quiz did not attend the review session. So some student in the class who completed the reading did not attend the review session.

Every vehicle in the city fleet that runs on diesel is inspected annually. Every vehicle that is inspected annually is kept in the north garage. So every diesel vehicle in the city fleet is kept in the north garage.

No apprentice in the Garvey workshop is permitted to operate the lathe. Every worker who is permitted to operate the lathe has completed the workshop's safety training. So no apprentice in the workshop has completed that safety training.

Every Morrow Building tenant who keeps a pet has signed the pet agreement. No tenant who has signed it is exempt from the cleaning fee. So any Morrow Building tenant exempt from the cleaning fee keeps no pet.
questions.explanation: The argument runs: all A are B; no B is C; so any C is not A (a valid chain stated in contrapositive form). E matches term for term: pet keepers sign the agreement, no signer is exempt, so any exempt tenant keeps no pet. C is tempting because it is also a valid all-all chain, but it has no 'no' premise and does not conclude in contrapositive form; A, B, and D are invalid.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Any unmonitored troop doesn't forage in the orchards.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Orchard foragers → shed raiders; shed raiders → monitored.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: All A are B; no B is C; so any C is not A (orchard foragers → shed raiders → monitored; so unmonitored → not a forager).

breakdown.analysis: Chain it: forages (A) → raids sheds (B) → monitored (not C). Contrapositive of the whole chain: not monitored (C) → doesn't forage (not A). So the shape is: all A are B; no B is C; therefore any C is not A. It's valid. We need an answer with an 'all' premise, a 'no' premise, and a conclusion that starts from the last term and denies the first.

choices.note: Same opening shape, but the conclusion is wrong. The premises give: pre-1990 → strings → not radio edit, so a radio-edit song was NOT recorded before 1990. This concludes the reverse, so it's invalid.
Uses 'some' instead of 'no,' and the conclusion doesn't follow: the students who skipped the review needn't be ones who did the reading. Different and invalid.
Tempting, because it's also a valid chain. But it's all-all-all with a straightforward conclusion. No 'no' premise and no contrapositive conclusion, so the pattern differs.
Invalid: apprentices can't use the lathe, but people who can't use it may still have taken the training. The structure (no A is B; all B are C; so no A is C) is different.
CORRECT. Pet → signed agreement → not exempt. Contrapositive: exempt → no pet. All A are B; no B is C; any C is not A. A perfect match.

questions.stimulus: A survey asked every parent of a child between the ages of three and six in the town of Brell to compare the amount of time their own child spends on screens with the amounts spent by the other surveyed parents' children. Each surveyed parent has exactly one child in that age range. Most of the parents said they believe their own child spends less time on screens than do most of the other surveyed parents' children.
questions.stem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?
choices: Most of the surveyed parents are mistaken about how much time their own children spend on screens.
Not every surveyed parent who holds this belief about his or her child's screen time is correct.
Surveyed parents tend to underestimate the amount of time that their own children spend on screens.
The surveyed parents whose children spend the most time on screens are the ones most likely to be mistaken.
Children between the ages of three and six in Brell spend less time on screens than same-age children elsewhere do.
questions.explanation: At most about half of the children can spend less screen time than most of the others, yet most parents believe their child does, so at least some of those parents must be wrong (B). A is the attractive trap: the arithmetic shows only that some believers are wrong, not that most parents are, and C goes further by assuming the errors come from underestimating their own child's time rather than, say, overestimating other children's.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Every Brell parent of a 3-to-6-year-old was surveyed, one child each; 2. Most parents believe their child spends less screen time than most of the other children.

breakdown.analysis: Hard to prephrase until you do the math. Line the children up by screen time. A child who spends less than 'most of the others' has to be in roughly the bottom half. So at most about half the children can truly fit that description. But more than half the parents believe their child does. So some of those believers must be wrong. How many? We only know 'some.' 'Many' isn't 'all,' and 'some are wrong' isn't 'most are wrong.' We need a modest answer: at least one believer is mistaken.

choices.note: Tempting, and it's the classic trap here. If, say, 55 percent believe it and 49 percent are actually below most others, only about 6 percent need be wrong. 'Most are mistaken' doesn't follow.
CORRECT. More parents hold the belief than can possibly be right, so not all of them are correct. Modest and guaranteed by the numbers.
Assumes the direction of the error. A wrong parent could be overestimating the other children's screen time rather than underestimating their own child's.
Plausible, but nothing in the survey tells us which parents are wrong. We don't know this.
The survey compares Brell children only with each other. Children elsewhere are never mentioned. New information.

questions.stimulus: Literary scholar: Late in his life, the poet Anselm Rook revised many of his early poems before including them in his collected works, and most readers today know those poems only in their revised versions. Scholars who want to understand how Rook's style developed over his career should therefore study the versions of the early poems that were first published, rather than the revised versions.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the literary scholar's argument depends?
choices: The versions of Rook's early poems that were first published are of higher literary quality than the revised versions.
Rook revised his early poems many years after they were first published, when his style had already matured.
Most readers of Rook's collected works are unaware that many of the early poems in it were revised.
At least some of Rook's revisions altered stylistic features of the early poems he revised.
Rook's style changed more during the early part of his career than it did at any later point.
questions.explanation: The recommendation to study the original versions makes sense only if the revisions altered the style in some way; if no revision changed any stylistic feature, the revised versions would reveal Rook's early style just as well, so D is required. B is the attractive trap: the stimulus says the revisions came late in life, but the argument doesn't depend on any particular gap in time or on his style having matured, only on the revisions' having changed the style.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Scholars studying Rook's stylistic development should study the first-published versions of his early poems, not the revised ones.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Late in life Rook revised many early poems for his collected works; most readers know only the revised versions.

breakdown.analysis: Why would the originals matter for studying style? Only if the revisions changed the style. If Rook just fixed typos, the revised versions would show his early style perfectly well. We need a modest answer: the revisions changed at least some stylistic features. Then run the negation test on each choice.

choices.note: Wrong dimension: quality, not style. The originals could be worse poems and still be the better record of early style. Negating it doesn't hurt.
choices.negation: The first-published versions are not of higher literary quality than the revised versions.

choices.note: Tempting, because it echoes 'late in his life.' But the argument doesn't need a long gap or a matured style. Even revisions made soon after publication would matter, as long as they changed the style. Negating it leaves the argument standing.
choices.negation: Rook did not revise his early poems many years after first publication, or his style had not yet matured when he did.

choices.note: What readers know is irrelevant to what scholars should study. Negating it changes nothing.
choices.negation: At least half of the readers of the collected works know that many early poems were revised.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: none of the revisions changed any stylistic feature. Then the revised versions show the early style just as well, and there's no reason to prefer the originals. The argument collapses.
choices.negation: None of Rook's revisions altered any stylistic feature of the poems he revised.

choices.note: Too strong and not needed. The scholars want to understand his development, whenever the biggest changes came. Negating it is harmless.
choices.negation: Rook's style changed at least as much at some later point as in the early part of his career.

questions.stimulus: Every painting in the Ostrander collection is insured, as are about half of the sculptures in the collection. Some of the insured works in the collection are currently on loan to other museums. So some of the works now on loan are paintings, and some are sculptures.
questions.stem: The flawed pattern of reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to that in the argument above?
choices: Every trail in Harlan Park is maintained by volunteers, as are about half of the park's campgrounds. None of the areas maintained by volunteers is open in winter. So no trail in the park is open in winter, and neither is any campground that volunteers maintain.
Every sedan on Corbin's lot has a warranty, as do about half of the trucks on the lot. The vehicle that Ms. Avila bought from the lot has a warranty. So it must be either a sedan or a truck.

Most of the poems in the Brightwater anthology rhyme, and most of the poems in that same anthology are sonnets written in English. So at least some of the English sonnets in the Brightwater anthology rhyme.
Every fern in the Ashby greenhouse needs daily misting, as do about half of the orchids grown there. So about half of the plants in the Ashby greenhouse that need daily misting must be orchids.

Every apprentice at the Renfrew print shop has taken the safety course, as have about half of its delivery drivers. Some employees who have taken the course work nights. So some night workers are apprentices, and some are delivery drivers.
questions.explanation: The argument assumes that because all paintings and some sculptures fall into the insured group, and some insured works are on loan, the loaned works must include both kinds; but the insured works on loan could all be paintings, or all sculptures. E repeats this exact overlap error. B is tempting because it uses the same opening premise, but its flaw is overlooking other kinds of vehicles; A and C are valid inferences, so they can't match a flawed argument.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Some loaned works are paintings, and some are sculptures.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: All paintings are insured; about half the sculptures are insured; some insured works are on loan.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: All A and some B are C; some C are D; so some D are A and some D are B.

breakdown.analysis: Picture the insured group: all the paintings plus half the sculptures. 'Some' of that group is on loan. Which ones? Could be only paintings. Could be only sculptures. Knowing that some members of a mixed group have a feature doesn't tell you that members of each kind have it. We need an answer with the same overlap mistake: all A and some B are C; some C are D; so some D are A and some are B.

choices.note: Same opening shape, but the reasoning is valid: if no volunteer-maintained area opens in winter, every trail (all volunteer-maintained) and every volunteer-maintained campground is closed. A valid version can't match a flawed original.

Tempting, because the first sentence is a near-copy. But the flaw differs: the lot might sell vans or SUVs with warranties. That's overlooking other categories, not assuming a 'some' group contains both kinds.
Valid. If more than half the poems rhyme and more than half are English sonnets, the two groups must overlap. No flaw to match.
Flawed, but differently: it draws a proportion ('about half') from numbers it doesn't have, with no 'some of the group' step. Different structure.

CORRECT. All apprentices and half the drivers took the course; some course-takers work nights; so some night workers are apprentices and some are drivers. The night workers could all be apprentices. Same error, same shape.

questions.stimulus: Last winter the price of firewood in the Halvik region rose sharply. Most households in Halvik heat their homes with natural gas, and early last winter the price of natural gas rose steeply. Many of these households, facing higher gas bills, probably turned to wood stoves for heat, and it was this added demand for firewood that drove up its price.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?
choices: The price of natural gas in Halvik fell somewhat late last winter but stayed well above its level of the year before.
Some households in Halvik heat their homes with electricity rather than with either natural gas or wood.
Last winter, gas-heated Halvik households burned far more firewood than usual, while wood-only households burned their usual amount.
Last winter in Halvik was colder, and lasted longer, than any other winter in the previous decade.
Firewood prices also rose sharply last winter in neighboring regions where few households heat with natural gas.
questions.explanation: C confirms the proposed mechanism: the extra firewood demand came specifically from gas-heating households, while wood-only households, unaffected by gas prices, did not increase their use. D is tempting because a cold winter would raise demand for firewood, but that is a rival explanation that does not depend on gas prices, so it weakens the argument; E likewise points to a cause other than gas prices.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Gas households switching to wood drove up the price of firewood.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Firewood prices rose sharply; most households heat with gas; gas prices rose steeply early in the winter; many gas households probably turned to wood.

breakdown.analysis: The argument names a specific mechanism: gas got expensive, gas households burned wood, demand rose, price rose. What else could raise firewood prices? A cold winter, a supply problem, a regional shortage. A strong strengthener confirms the mechanism itself, showing the extra demand came from exactly the households the argument points to. Watch for answers that raise demand for a different reason; those are rival causes.

choices.note: Gas stayed expensive, so this doesn't hurt. But it adds nothing either; we already know gas prices rose steeply.
Electric-heat households are outside the mechanism. Irrelevant.

CORRECT. The extra wood was burned by the gas households, and the wood-only households, who didn't face higher gas bills, didn't burn more. That's the mechanism, confirmed, with a built-in comparison group.
Tempting, because a cold winter raises demand for firewood. But that's a rival cause that works without gas prices. It weakens the argument; it doesn't strengthen it.
Firewood prices rose even where gas isn't used, so something other than gas prices could be at work. This weakens the argument.

questions.stimulus: Hospital administrator: Two years ago, our hospital began requiring that every medication order be double-checked by a pharmacist before the medication is given to a patient. Since then, the number of medication errors reported each year has fallen by 40 percent. So the double-check rule has substantially reduced the harm that medication errors cause our patients.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the administrator's argument?
choices: Since the rule took effect, the hospital has made it considerably easier for staff to report medication errors anonymously.
Pharmacists at the hospital now spend considerably more of their working time checking medication orders than they did before.
Medication errors are reported more often at hospitals that do not require pharmacists to double-check orders than at hospitals that do.
Nearly all medication errors that seriously harm patients occur when drugs are administered, not when they are ordered.
Several other hospitals in the region adopted similar double-check rules at about the same time and saw similar declines.
questions.explanation: The evidence is a drop in the number of reported errors, but the conclusion is about harm; D shows that the harmful errors arise at a stage the order check does not touch, so the errors the rule eliminated may be the harmless ones and the harm may not have fallen. A is tempting because reporting changes often undermine such arguments, but easier reporting would make a 40 percent drop even more impressive, strengthening the argument.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The double-check rule substantially reduced the harm medication errors cause patients.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Since the rule began, reported medication errors fell 40 percent.

breakdown.analysis: Is the number of errors really the measure of harm? One serious error can outweigh a hundred trivial ones. The evidence counts errors; the conclusion is about harm. That's a measure mismatch, counts versus severity. We need an answer showing the drop could be all in harmless errors, while the harmful ones carry on untouched.

choices.note: Tempting, because a change in reporting usually spoils before-and-after numbers. But here reporting got easier, which should push reported errors up. A 40 percent drop despite that looks even better. This strengthens.
Shows the rule takes pharmacists' time. A cost of the rule, not evidence about whether it reduced harm.
Fits the idea that double-checking cuts errors. If anything it supports the administrator.

CORRECT. The rule checks orders. If the harmful errors happen at administration, the rule can't catch them, so the errors it removed were the ones that weren't hurting anyone. Fewer errors, same harm.
Other hospitals seeing similar drops after similar rules suggests the rule works. It doesn't touch the jump from errors to harm.

questions.stimulus: Art market analyst: Ten years ago, works by living artists accounted for 40 percent of the total value of the art sold at the Ferrand auction house. Last year, they accounted for only 25 percent. Clearly, collectors at Ferrand are spending less on works by living artists than they did a decade ago.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the analyst's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: presumes that the collectors who buy at Ferrand are representative of art collectors in general
confuses the number of works by living artists sold at Ferrand with the total value of those works
takes for granted that works by living artists are generally less expensive than works by artists who have died
presumes, without providing justification, that the prices of individual works by living artists have fallen
overlooks the possibility that the total value of art sold at Ferrand has grown substantially
questions.explanation: A smaller share of a larger total can be a larger amount: if Ferrand's total sales doubled, 25 percent of the new total would exceed 40 percent of the old. E names this overlooked possibility. B is tempting because it sounds like the classic number-versus-value error, but the analyst uses value consistently throughout; the confusion is between a share and an absolute amount.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Collectors at Ferrand are spending less on works by living artists than a decade ago.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Living artists' share of Ferrand's total sales value fell from 40 percent to 25 percent.

breakdown.analysis: A smaller slice, sure. But of what size pie? Spending is an absolute amount; 40 and 25 percent are shares. If the pie grew, a smaller slice can still be bigger. Try numbers: $10 million total then, 40 percent = $4 million; $20 million now, 25 percent = $5 million. Spending went up. We need an answer that says the total may have grown.

choices.note: The conclusion is only about collectors at Ferrand. Nothing generalizes to collectors in general, so representativeness is irrelevant.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Collectors at Ferrand prefer landscapes, so most collectors everywhere prefer landscapes.

choices.note: Tempting, because it sounds like the classic error. But the analyst talks about value from start to finish; the number of works never appears. The real confusion is share versus amount.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: We sold more paintings this year than last, so our painting revenue rose.

choices.note: The argument never compares prices of living and dead artists' works, and doesn't need to.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Living artists' works sell for less, so Ferrand should stop selling them.

choices.note: The conclusion is about total spending, not about prices of individual works. The argument doesn't need prices to have fallen; fewer sales at the same prices would do.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Spending on living artists fell, so each of their paintings must now sell for less.

choices.note: CORRECT. If the total grew enough, 25 percent of it can be more money than 40 percent of the old total. The argument treats a falling share as falling spending.
